title: Denver Film Festival Unveils Lineup and Honorees
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 7:00am Anthony Ippolito stars as Sylvester Stallone in I Play Rocky Claire Folger/Amazon Content Services This year’s Denver Film Festival has fallen into view. Denver Film today unveiled the roster of movies and boldfaced name honorees that will make up the 49th edition of the Colorado capital city’s marquee film event, which is scheduled for Oct. 22-Nov. 1. In all, 129 features, documentaries and shorts will hit screens inside the Sie FilmCenter, Ellie Caulkins Opera House, MCA Denver at the Holiday Theater, and the Denver Museum of Nature & Science. The fest will open with Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky starring Anthony Ippolito (as Sylvester Stallone) at Ellie Caulkins Opera House (with writer Peter Gamble in attendance and participating in a later conversation), and close with James Gray ‘s Paper Tiger starring Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller at the MCA Denver at the Holiday Theater. Centerpiece picks in between include Danny Boyle’s Ink starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy, and Tony Gilroy ‘s Behemoth! starring Pedro Pascal as a gifted cellist. Related Stories Movies 'Avengers: Endgame' Powers $26M Return at Crowded Box Office Movies James Gray on Broader Takeaways From Personal Film 'Paper Tiger': "What Connects Us Is What Matters" Paper Tiger Cannes Film Festival The special presentations section features many standout films from the fall festival circuit and beyond. Those selections include (in alphabetical order) Stephanie Ahn’s Bedford Park , Siân Heder’s Being Heumann , Pedro Almodóvar’s Bitter Christmas , Jordan Firstman’s Club Kid , Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut , Simon Stone’s Elsinore , Marie Kreutzer’s Gentle Monster , Beth de Araújo’s Josephine , Guy Nattiv’s The Liberation , Andrew Haigh’s A Long Winter, Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York , Brad Bird’s animated Ray Gunn , Liz Sargent’s Take Me Home , Anton Corbijn’s A Talent for Murder , Leah Nelson’s animated Tangles , Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fisher’s Wicker , and Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine. Club Kid A24 It’s worth noting that the showings of Josephine and Take Me Home are being co-presented with the Sundance Film Festival, which is heading to Denver Film Festival’s backyard in Boulder, Colorado in 2027. Also notable: Other picks include standout international films like TIFF’s People Choice Award winner La Bola Negra from Netflix, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s All of a Sudden , and Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur which won a Grand Prix in Cannes. Speaking of awards, Denver Film will dole out a few during the fest’s run. Carrie Coon has been tapped to receive an excellence in acting award for her thus far critically acclaimed work in The Liberation as a woman who stuns her family by joining a cult led by Lily James. John Cho will be feted with an Outlaw Award for work opposite Mahershala Ali in Y our Mother Your Mother Your Mother. Sargent will take a spin in the spotlight as breakthrough director for Take Me Home , which was based on her short film of the same name about a woman caring for her aging parents. Fred Hechinger, who broke out in The White Lotus and Gladiator II , will receive a rising star prize after a screening of his latest, A Long Winter. Others set to receive awards include Benedetta Porcaroli with a Maglione Italian Film Award for The Kidnapping of Arabella , David Acord with an excellence in sound design for Behemoth!, and experimental filmmaker Michael Gitlin will accept an annual Stan Brakhage Award, presented along with a retrospective of his work. Carrie Coon in The Liberation Courtesy Bleecker Street Some other notable titles among this year’s selections are Ron Howard’s Avedon , Nanette Burstein’s Carl Sagan: We Are Made of Star Stuff , Lukas Dhont’s Coward , Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Petra Volpe’s Frank & Louis , Rachel J. Morrison’s Joybubbles , Ken Russell’s The Devils , Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love , Markus Schleinzer’s Rose starring Sandra Hüller, Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care, Barbara Kopple’s Union Town, Dawn Porter’s When a Witness Recants , and Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fisher’s Wicker . “This year’s program highlights the remarkable ways cinema captures human connection and resilience, and it delivers a lineup that is as entertaining as it is thought-provoking,” explained Denver Film Festival artistic director Matthew Campbell. “From sharp, high-altitude Colorado comedies to award-winning festival circuit fare, captivating documentaries and stories born here in our own community, these films demonstrate the pure joy and impact of great storytelling. We’re looking forward to welcoming our audiences to experience this dynamic mix of bold international cinema, new voices and brilliant local talent.” Added Denver Film CEO Kevin Smith: “Forty-nine years in, the Denver Film Festival is still driven by what has always mattered most: bringing our community together around great movies and the people who make them. We’re incredibly proud to be a long-standing part of Denver’s vibrant arts and cultural landscape and I can’t imagine a better way to open our 49th Festival than with I Play Rocky , an underdog story that captures the determination, creativity and spirit of independent film we celebrate every year.” The film festival is funded by the Colorado Office of Film and Television, Bonfils Stanton Foundation, Denver Arts & Venues and SCFD (Scientific and Cultural Facilities District) with media sponsors CBS Colorado, Axios, City Cast Denver, Colorado Public Radio, Denverse, Metromode, Rocky Mountain Public Media, and marquee sponsors William LaBahn, Epicurean, Next50, Amazon, AOR, Halcyon, Sheila K. O’Brien, Crusonia Wealth Advisors, Dormer Harpring, LLC, Anna and John Sie Foundation, Betsy Mordecai Heyman and Gareth Heyman, Julie Mordecai, Mercedes-Benz of Denver, and HW Home. The full lineup — including documentaries, shorts and more — can be found here , including intel on tickets. Fun fact: The Denver Arts & Venues and the 2026 Arts Complex Creates grant program makes it so that all three public screenings at the Ellie Caulkins Opera House will be offered with an allotment of sliding-scale “Pay-What-You-Can” admissions. title: Will ‘The Shards’ Return? FX Show Tests Ryan Murphy’s Sway In Disney Empire
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All October 3, 2026 6:02am Kaia Gerber and Homer Gere in FX's 'The Shards.' Everett Logo text As The Shards hit screens in early August, Ryan Murphy spoke about how he and author Bret Easton Ellis saw the series potentially running for several seasons. It will have to get to season two first — and on that front, The Shards remains in limbo. Three-plus weeks out from the season finale, which ended on a sizable cliffhanger, there’s been no word from FX on the show’s status. That’s not necessarily a bad sign: The Disney-owned outlet has been known to take its time on renewal decisions. Pickups for Adults and The Lowdown , to name two recent critically acclaimed shows, came months after their first seasons ended. FX and Murphy also seem to have an understanding that when he’s ready with an idea, they’re ready to back it. Two-plus years passed between the last season of American Horror Story and the one that premiered Sept. 24. There was a nearly seven -year gap between seasons one and two of Feud . Those are anthology series, however, and one season doesn’t necessarily flow directly from the previous one (the large pile-up of AHS lore aside). The Shards is intended as an ongoing show, following the same set of characters over a long time. Murphy has also spoken about how much he personally connected to The Shards, even though Ellis’ novel — about a group of L.A. prep school kids in the early ’80s and a possible serial killer in their midst — is semi-autobiographical (not the serial killer parts, obviously). “My pitch to him was that 1981, the year the book is set, was the most important year of my life in many ways,” Murphy told The Hollywood Reporter about how he sold Ellis on working together. “That was the year I turned 16. That was my first date. My first driving lesson. I lost my virginity. On and on and on. I really understood those kids, and particularly, the Bret character.” Compounding the mystery is the fact that no one outside of Disney really knows how well The Shards performed for FX and Hulu. Linear ratings were small — an average of 237,000 viewers for initial airings on FX — but that’s par for the course for a scripted cable series now. A great majority of the show’s audience will come from streaming, but The Shards never made Nielsen’s streaming top 10s and FX hasn’t released any of its own data. Neither of those facts is out of the ordinary either: Most FX shows don’t break into the streaming charts, and the outlet rarely does ratings PR. The Shards is also the second Murphy-produced FX show this year to end on a cliffhanger and not (as yet) be picked up. The Beauty wrapped its season in early March with a lot of loose threads; in July, the show’s cast was released. ( Love Story , which FX did point to as a ratings success, also hasn’t been renewed, but it may fall under the aforementioned “when the right idea hits” plan for Murphy’s anthologies.) Murphy has a big overall deal with Disney’s 20th Television and a long working relationship with both the studio and FX — even when he was based at Netflix, his 20th-produced shows continued to churn out new seasons. If The Shards does get a second season, it may be a testament to those relationships more so than the validation of a big hit. THR

title: Projeto Paradiso Founder Olga Rabinovich to Receive Inaugural Encounters Award at the São Paulo Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 6:01am PT Projeto Paradiso Founder Olga Rabinovich to Receive Inaugural Encounters Award at the São Paulo Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) The inaugural honor recognizes Rabinovich’s work supporting the development and international reach of Brazilian film talent through Projeto Paradiso By Rafa Sales Ross Plus Icon Rafa Sales Ross Guest Contributor Latest Globoplay Greenlights Adaptation of Raphael Montes’ ‘Uma Mulher no Escuro,’ From Banijay Entertainment’s A Fábrica Brazilian Banner (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago Producer-Led The Creatives Enters Jointly Owned Holding Structure as Anton Studios Joins as Partner and Minority Investor (EXCLUSIVE) 3 days ago Anna Kendrick ‘Over the Moon’ About Directing ‘The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo,’ Compares ‘Pitch Perfect’ Friendships to the Avengers 6 days ago See All Courtesy of Projeto Paradiso Philanthropist Olga Rabinovich will receive the inaugural Prêmio Encontros (Encounters Award) at this year’s Encontro de Ideias Audiovisuais, the industry platform of the São Paulo International Film Festival. The award honors her enduring commitment to advancing Brazilian cinema and elevating the international profile of Brazilian film and talent through her work with Projeto Paradiso . The Encounters Award was created to spotlight the transformative role of private investment in culture, bringing together private funders and the creative professionals behind audiovisual productions. The inaugural honor will be bestowed upon Rabinovich during the event’s opening gala ceremony on Oct. 14 and ahead of an in-conversation event with Neon president Jeff Deutchman. Related Stories 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation Born in São Paulo, Rabinovich spent years volunteering in hospitals, working closely with terminally ill patients. In 2018, she founded the Olga Rabinovich Institute, launching Projeto Paradiso soon after. The initiative is dedicated to the advancement of the Brazilian audiovisual sector and grew out of her belief that “stories can change the world,” as well as a decision to invest in the people who create them and want to share them with audiences worldwide. Popular on Variety “Olga Rabinovich is the first recipient of the newly created Prêmio Encontros, because she was the inspiration behind the award,” said Renata de Almeida, director of the São Paulo International Film Festival. I first heard Olga’s name in early 2018, when Josephine Bourgois came to see me about someone from the private sector who wanted to create an institute dedicated to cinema. The Olga Rabinovich Institute was announced during the 42nd Mostra, bringing a breath of hope at a time that promised to be particularly difficult for Brazilian film and culture.” “Eight years later, Projeto Paradiso, an initiative of the Olga Rabinovich Institute, has already made a major contribution to discovering and championing a new generation of talent, strengthening Brazil ’s audiovisual sector as a whole,” continued the director. “Projeto Paradiso has an outstanding professional team, as its results clearly demonstrate. But the image that stays with me is of a meeting with Olga, climbing the winding stairs of our little building for a somewhat chaotic coffee in the festival’s office. Because, in the end, almost everything really does begin with an encounter.” Courtesy of Milena Palladino Earlier this year, Variety sat down with the philanthropist ahead of the third Projeto Paradiso National Network Meeting in Brazil’s buzzy production hub of Recife . Rabinovich said she “loved the idea of supporting cinema because I feel it is a magical art form.” “You enter a screening room without knowing whether you’ll be elated or disturbed or moved. It’s a transformative experience. I think it’s incredible to have a communal artistic experience that moves you like this.” Projeto Paradiso offers a wide range of support to Brazilian screen professionals to maximize their presence on the global stage, supporting the development of stories through fellowships, residencies, workshops, and other training and international reach initiatives. The Paradiso Talent Network now comprises 278 Brazilian professionals. The organization also helps connect Brazilian talent and projects with the international industry through a network of more than 250 partner institutions in Brazil and abroad, including the Hubert Bals Fund, La Fabrique Cinéma de l’Institut français, TorinoFilmLab, Film Independent and the Sundance Institute. The initiative was recently behind buzzy festival titles such as Allan Deberton’s Berlinale-winning “Gugu’s World” and Grace Passô’s “Our Secret,” and boasts a talent network of 264 professionals, including Anita Rocha da Silveira (“Medusa”), Juliana Rojas (“Good Manners”) and Dira Paes (“Manas”). In 2025 Projeto Paradiso teamed with the Embratur Brazilian Tourism Board to launch Screen Brasil, offering four Brazilian films a year in two calls – the latest of which closed Oct. 2 supporting their international distribution campaigns, submissions being made by the international sales agent holding the film’s commercial rights. Announced at Cannes Marché du Film this May, films backed to date take in Gabriel Mascaro’s “The Blue Trail,” Rafaela Camelo’s “The Nature of Invisible Things” and animated feature “Papaya.” Projeto Paradiso’s relationship with the São Paulo International Film Festival dates back to 2018, when the philanthropy initiatve was launched during the festival’s 42nd edition. Since then, Projeto Paradiso has steadily expanded its presence at the festival. Since 2023, it has presented the annual Paradiso Distribution Support Award, providing a distribution grant for the theatrical release of a fiction feature. In 2024, Projeto Paradiso was also one of the driving forces behind a new partnership with the Hubert Bals Fund (HBF), which led to the creation of HBF+Brazil following initial discussions at Encontro de Ideias. The 50th edition of the São Paulo International Film Festival runs Oct. 15-29. ‘Wildwood,’ ‘I Play Rocky,’ ‘Behemoth’ and More Among AFI Fest 2026 Lineup Edmund Yeo and Vivian Sung Chase Malaysia’s Buried Past in Toronto Title ‘The Age of Goodbyes’: ‘Ordinary People Living Inside History’ ‘Father Father’ Director on Doc About a Gay Israeli-Palestinian Couple Who Have a Child on Eve of Oct. 7: It’s a ‘Beautiful Lesson Right Now’ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘La Bola Negra’ Star Guitarricadelafuente to Receive Discovery Award at SCAD Savannah Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3 Stars Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries, Aryan Simhadri, Set to Attend Italy’s Lucca Comics and Games India’s ‘Angh’ Wins Toronto Platform Award, Nabs Automatic Oscar Contention Loading comments...

title: Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly?
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 6:00am PT Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly? By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest Skydance Blasts Off: Can David Ellison Make Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Fly? 51 minutes ago Disney Licenses Slew of Titles to Netflix, Including All Five ‘Ice Age’ Movies, ‘Percy Jackson and the Olympians,’ ‘Felicity,’ ‘Will Trent,’ ‘Elio’ and More (EXCLUSIVE) 23 hours ago New Name of Paramount-Warner Bros. Unveiled: Skydance 1 day ago See All Getty Images; Courtesy of Skydance Corp. David Ellison has emerged victorious. And he’s boldly — or arrogantly, if you prefer — decided to name the entertainment giant that he’s bolted together Skydance Corp., nodding to the original name of his film production firm that has swallowed up two Hollywood studios over the past 14 months. Defying skeptics and beating back opponents, Ellison has harpooned his white whale in buying Warner Bros. Discovery. Now he has to prove that the $111 billion mega-merger can become a profitable entertainment powerhouse, and not just a vessel that will get sucked under by a massive whirlpool of debt. Related Stories 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation As the closing of the deal — set to occur Tuesday, Oct. 6 — became a certainty, entertainment industry insiders started to come to grips with the reality that the enlarged company is a new and unpredictable force in town. The deal has been polarizing for the creative community, with many boldface names going public in their opposition to the merger. The new leadership team that Skydance is assembling under the direction of Ellison and Ynon Kreiz, just recruited from Mattel to serve as co-CEO, has to navigate that dynamic. And they must do it while walking a tightrope on Wall Street to pay down debt and grow profits across film, linear TV and streaming. Popular on Variety “They need to move as quickly as possible to get the leverage down,” says Jawad Hussain, managing director at S&P Global. “The biggest hurdle and the biggest thing we’re going to be keeping our eye on is integration and execution.” Two years ago, Hussain says, Skydance Meida was a small company that turned out a few films a year. “Now it’s managing one of the largest media companies. It’s not necessarily an easy task.” Related Stories Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’ New Name of Paramount-Warner Bros. Unveiled: Skydance Skydance Says It’s Committed to L.A., but Threat to Leave Has Proved Potent George Cheeks May Be Poised for Expanded TV Role at Skydance Post Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger European Entertainment Leaders Mostly Optimistic About David Ellison’s Takeover of Warner Bros.: ‘I Believe in His Commitment to Cinema’ It’s all been a whirlwind. On the morning of Sept. 30, Ellison still didn’t know if it was a done deal. He had spent more than a year in his relentless pursuit of acquiring Warner Bros. and HBO. The WBD board rejected his takeover offers eight times. David Zaslav, Warner Bros. Discovery’s boss, ghosted Ellison in December 2025 after Netflix clinched a deal for WB’s streaming and studios business. But Ellison didn’t surrender; he finally outbid Netflix in February , with a $31/share offer that was nearly 2.5 times the stock price before the M&A frenzy kicked off. It was an offer WBD couldn’t refuse. Ellison and his legal team, headed by former DOJ official Makan Delrahim, predicted the proposed Paramount-WB combo would easily clear regulatory approvals. In June, Trump’s Justice Department rubber-stamped the pact without attaching any conditions. All told, regulators in 68 jurisdictions worldwide cleared the merger with minimal pushback. The last barricade in Ellison’s way? An antitrust lawsuit brought by 12 Democratic state attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta. Ellison believed the litigation was politically motivated, stoked by fears he would try to turn CNN into a Trump-friendly mouthpiece. (He has repeatedly promised a hands-off approach to CNN’s news coverage.) But the AGs pressed their case and a federal judge agreed that their arguments — that Paramount-Warner Bros. would wield undue power in theatrical and basic cable markets — had merit. A trial was scheduled to begin in March 2027. Frustrated and incredulous, Ellison let it be known through press leaks in August that he would pull Paramount out of California if the state AGs didn’t let him close the WB deal. Paramount insiders continue to insist the notion of Ellison’s Golden State exit wasn’t a bluff or a threat. Bonta, seeming to realize he would gain no political capital by derailing or delaying the merger, relented. Paramount and the AGs announced a settlement of the suit on Sept. 21 — with a list of concessions so lenient that it surprised not only industry watchers but also employees at both companies . Now all that was left was the judge’s approval of the settlement. Worryingly for Ellison, U.S. District Court Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin at a Sept. 24 hearing had left the door open to a potential further third-party review of the settlement at the behest of Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.). The groups behind the #BlockTheMerger coalition, which had amassed more than 5,700 signatories from actors, filmmakers and industry workers opposed to the deal, filed a brief with the court urging Martínez-Olguín to reject the settlement. But on Sept. 30 at just after 12:30 p.m pacific time, the judge issued her ruling: She had approved the settlement . The proposed consent decree, Martínez-Olguin wrote, reflects a “compromise that may leave some dissatisfaction for both sides and the public but a compromise that saves the risk, time and expense of litigating through trial.” Boom! Teams at both companies swung into action to make the final preparations needed to close the deal. That evening, Paramount and WBD confirmed the merger’s expected closing date of Oct. 6, at which point Paramount’s common stock will move from Nasdaq to list on the New York Stock Exchange. The stock symbol will change from “PSKY” to “SKYD,” reflecting the Skydance corporate name. Ellison is expected to lead a town hall meeting with employees next Tuesday, and Ellison and Kreiz are scheduled to host a virtual press briefing — along with the new Skydance’s executive leadership — at 7 p.m. ET on Oct. 6. Coincidentally, on Sept. 30 Ellison had been sitting on his own bit of hot news: He was ready to announce that he recruited media vet Kreiz to be co-CEO at the combined Paramount-WBD. The merged entity’s businesses will jointly report to Ellison and Kreiz. Word of Kreiz’s joining Paramount trickled out earlier in the day, but Ellison had already decided to wait until after market close to announce it. Paramount put the release on the wire at 1:06 p.m. , a little over half an hour after the judge OK’d the antitrust settlement. Ellison triumphantly sent Paramount employees a companywide email about Kreiz’s hiring, timestamped at 1:18 p.m., praising the exec as a “proven builder and operator.” Kreiz, during his eight years at Mattel, had helped cut costs through layoffs — and oversaw its first theatrical release, 2023 blockbuster “Barbie.” He swung the company to profitability, but revenue has stubbornly stayed flat the last four years. Ellison wrote in his email: “Together we are well positioned to integrate, operationalize and run the businesses as we build one of the most ambitious next-generation media companies in the industry’s history. Kreiz, as part of his compensation package, will receive $31.5 million in fully vested stock as a signing bonus with the merger close. Then on Friday, Oct. 2, Ellison shared on X that the new corporation would be … Skydance . His post included a sizzle reel of the combined company’s biggest hits, leading off with a clip from “Titanic” — an inauspicious choice, perhaps, given how that infamous voyage turned out. “Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture,” Ellison wrote. “By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history — we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.” Three years ago, Ellison was primarily known as a rich kid — scion of Oracle billionaire Larry Ellison, one of the world’s richest people — and a semi-successful movie producer, most notably with 2022’s “Top Gun: Maverick,” which turned in a boffo $1.5 billion at the box office. Now, having bagged Warner Bros., he can lay claim to being a titan in the business and no mere nepo baby. “Ellison stared down the attorneys general and won. He stared down the unions and won,” says Prof. Erik Gordon of University of Michigan’s Ross School of Business. “You can’t see David Ellison as daddy’s boy anymore. He’s a formidable force in the industry.” The Paramount-WBD merger is the biggest M&A deal in Hollywood history. It brings together two of Hollywood’s biggest movie studios, HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services dand TV brands including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, Food Network and more. The new company’s entertainment franchises span Harry Potter, Lord of the Rings, Game of Thrones and other HBO hits, the DC superhero universe, “Yellowstone,” “Mission: Impossible,” “Top Gun” and the Nickelodeon kids’ empire. “We still have work to do before the deal closes, and nothing changes until it does,” Ellison told employees in his memo about Kreiz. But even before the deal closed, the company’s new leadership was taking shape. Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy, co-heads of Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, will leave post-merger, sources told Variety . Paramount film heads Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein are in line to oversee both movie studios. With the deal close, Zaslav is expected to depart — with a boatload of money. Zaslav stands to earn at least $550 million in stock and cash once the Paramount-WBD deal closes, including $34.2 million in cash severance payments, per the terms of his “golden parachute” package. Skydance’s settlement-related obligations around theatrical film and the operation of its Paramount and Warner Bros. cable channels will undoubtedly have ripple effects in the marketplace that extend well beyond the U.S. Showbiz leaders in Europe have closely watched the transaction at a time when local-language production is at a peak thanks to the influence of Netflix, Amazon and Disney+. HBO has a growing international footprint that will be crucial to Skydance’s future growth. Pierre-Antoine Capton, chairman of France’s Mediawan, says the broader film and TV business is in line for a bumpy few years amid the shakeout of what he calls “a period of intense consolidation” of media assets. Mediawan bought Peter Chernin’s North Road Company earlier this year. It’s also circling Lionsgate as a potential acquisition. “Having spoken with David, I believe his vision is first and foremost an artistic, creative ambition,” Capton says of the Skydance merger. “He wants to build a more powerful group in order to invest in creation. It’s not only about making cuts. I believe in his commitment to cinema and to theatrical releases.” At the same time, “everywhere in the world we’re entering a much more difficult phase, where consolidation will be, in my view, one of the solutions to the economic problems we’re all going to face,” Capton says. Ellison and Kreiz will also be under pressure to deliver a clear roadmap for generating bigger profits from its streaming pillars, HBO Max and Paramount+. Casey Bloys, head of WBD’s HBO, is poised to assume oversight of the combined Paramount-Warner Bros. streaming business after Cindy Holland announced on Sept. 29 to staffers that she was stepping down from her role running Paramount+ and other direct-to-consumer businesses. Holland’s resignation blindsided some senior managers at Paramount, who thought Ellison had hired her for the long haul. “We all thought we had the home-court advantage — that David was bringing all the new people at Paramount to have them be part of Warner Bros.,” a company insider says. Paramount+ and HBO Max will together have more than 200 million subscribers. The newly merged Skydance can save money by consolidating its back-end streaming infrastructure. But “you don’t want to immediately combine the two streaming services because people won’t pay the sum of the two subscription prices,” says Prof. Sridhar Tayur of Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business. For the foreseeable future, HBO Max and Paramount+ will continue as discrete brands. Another area to watch: what Ellison does with CNN, which throws off operating cash that Skydance Corp. will need to bolster its finances. Ellison has held preliminary talks with CNN chief Mark Thompson about staying on after the merger, sources tell Variety . The prospect of Thompson continuing at the helm, at least for now, came as a relief to CNN personnel, who have been worried that Bari Weiss, the “anti-woke” media entrepreneur Ellison put in charge of CBS News, might extend her fiefdom to include the news cabler. Under the settlement with the 12-state coalition, the merged Paramount-Warner Bros. will be subject to monitoring by a “news editorial independence board.” The board, which will include representatives from the states, will establish which will establish “guiding editorial and journalism principles” for CNN and CBS News. But critics have dismissed this as a toothless condition. One player displeased with this outcome was Connecticut Attorney General William Tong, who, although he signed off on the settlement, said afterward he had advocated for a full divestiture of CNN and CBS News. Foes of ParaBros remain hopping mad. Actor Mark Ruffalo, one of the deal’s most strident critics, has vowed to continue the fight . “This merger will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost people their jobs — it is a bad deal for this country and should never have been approved,” he said in a social media post Sept. 30. Ruffalo’s feud with Paramount got ugly. On Aug. 21, he posted a message warning about the dangers of the Paramount-WB merger and alleged Larry Ellison’s Oracle was complicit in “what we now have come to see as a genocide” by the Israeli government against Palestinians. Paramount responded forcefully. A company rep asserted the “antisemitic tropes” Ruffalo invoked “aren’t just wrong — they’re a bridge too far.” Ruffalo has been set to reprise his role as an FBI agent in a second season of HBO’s “Task” crime drama. It remains to be seen if Ellison will let bygones be bygones. Apart from the shouting, the biggest burning questions about the new entity are about its financial condition. How is Paramount buying Warner Bros. Discovery, which has a market cap that’s six times larger? Paramount is issuing billions in debt securities and securing new loans to help foot the bill. Larry Ellison is bankrolling the WBD merger to the tune of $46.7 billion in equity financing. Paramount also lined up about $24 billion in commitments from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. In April, Paramount said the three Middle Eastern funds will own 38.5% of the combined entity, but that they will have no board seats or governance representation. The new company will be controlled by the Ellison family alongside Gerry Cardinale, founder and managing partner of RedBird Capital Partners. Cardinale’s firm is also pitching in equity for the WBD deal, after funding Skydance’s Paramount Global takeover. The new company’s net debt is estimated to be more than $80 billion. That staggering amount would translate into annual interest payments topping $6 billion. Add to that the fact that Paramount-WB, under the settlement with the AGs, is obligated to invest at least $300 million more on film production in the U.S. annually (above what the studios combined spent in 2025). Paramount execs have told Wall Street they can achieve $6 billion in cost savings through the merger. But not everyone thinks there’s $6 billion in cost savings to be squeezed out without negative consequences. There are obvious areas of overlap in corporate functions like IT, marketing, procurement and legal. But a big risk in executing a media merger of this scale is cutting into bone — resulting in the loss of creative professionals who are essential to the enterprise, says Prof. Tammy Madsen, a professor of management at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business. “Creativity matters,” Madsen says. “If you are too aggressive in eliminating redundancies in the creative parts of the company, you could kill the value.” Ellison, after the final clearance for the merger came through, wasn’t exactly popping the Champagne just yet. But he did, apparently, pop open some breakfast burritos. On Oct. 1 — out of nowhere — employees on the Paramount Studios lot in L.A. and at the company’s offices Burbank were welcomed with buffet breakfasts: French toast, pancakes, egg burritos, shakes, berry bowls, chia pudding and more. One insider says it was the first time they had ever seen the company put out that kind of spread. Perhaps it was more like a peace offering, coming before the pain of a first wave of layoffs at the new Skydance expected before the end of the year. The merger could result in the loss of some 4,500 film and TV jobs over three years in L.A. alone, according to a report issued by Los Angeles County in August. Insiders believe layoffs will continue with further rounds into 2027. There’s no way around the fact that thousands of employees across the former Paramount and WBD are about to get pink-slipped. But Ellison is betting that through the crucible of consolidation, a stronger company will emerge. “We have big goals for Skydance,” he wrote in his post on X about the new name, “and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks.” Marc Malkin, Michael Schneider, Cynthia Littleton, Elsa Keslassy, Matt Donnelly, Angelique Jackson, Brian Steinberg and Gene Maddaus contributed to this story. title: How a 100-Year-Old Indie Movie Theater Stays In Business
full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All October 3, 2026 5:01am Doreen Sayegh completed new renovations to reopen the Cranford Theater in Nov. 2019 — and then the pandemic hit. Courtesy Doreen Sayegh’s Cranford Theater, the last indie and family-run cinema in Union County, New Jersey, is about to turn 100. Sayegh, who owns the five-screen cinema in Cranford, near to New York City, will mark the centennial with a throwback screening of Padlocked, the silent film that opened the theater’s doors on November 29, 1926, with an accompanying organ player. But while honoring the legacy of her family in the exhibition business since the 1980s, Sayegh is just as committed to transforming the Cranford Theater with new programming and experiences to keep bringing customers through the door for the foreseeable future. “I want us to honor this incredible history while continuing to evolve and ask, what can the next 100 years look like?” Sayegh tells The Hollywood Reporter . As a child, she learned the cinema business alongside her father, Jesse Y. Sayegh. He ran an independent chain of movie theaters in New Jersey during the 1990s — when cinemas had far less competition for customers — and purchased the twin-screen Cranford Theater in 1997 from Cineplex Odeon and a year later reopened the indie cinema as a five-screen venue. “I sold my first popcorn at 8 years old, I could barely see over the concession counter,” she recalled, and sold her first movie tickets at age 11, before moving up the ranks as an usher, a box office cashier and eventually as a theater manager. Sayegh’s father, while retaining ownership of the building, sold the indie theater business in 2010, and she remained with the new owner, Bud Mayo’s Digiplex Destinations. But in 2019, after two other operators after Digiplex ran the theater, Sayegh, while showing a potential new tenant around the building, realized she wanted to make a go as its latest theater operator. “I was standing on the roof, looking out at the [Cranford] downtown and, I thought, ‘You know what? I want to do this. This is the right place for me,’” she recalled. So, with her father’s support, Sayegh completed new renovations to reopen the cinema complex in Nov. 2019, in time for the Christmas holidays. It wasn’t long, however, before the COVID-19 pandemic undid her best-laid plans. “By the time we got to March, the night before we closed down, we had maybe seven people in the building, and four of them were employees,” Sayegh recalls of that dark time. But, determined, she insists the pandemic was never to write the end of the story for the Cranford Theater. Instead, Sayegh got creative by, for example, handing through car doors fresh popcorn and candy to families pulling up at her front door to be consumed at home. And she transformed a parking lot she rented into a drive-in theater. “I was worried. You don’t know what’s going to happen,” she recounted of the new venture, which included an alert on her cellphone that sounded every time a ticket was sold. “I remember the day I was in the parking lot, in the heat and my phone started dinging as soon as the tickets went on sale. And then it just stopped,” Sayegh added. Suddenly, she feared only a couple of tickets had been sold, and her drive-in was a bust. So Sayegh rang her web hosting company to ask what had happened, only to be told surging ticket demand had crashed their servers. “You’re sold out. You sold out in 90 seconds, for three nights,” the report came back. The drive-in theater soon went to six nights a week of featuring classic movies on its outdoor screen. “That was so special to me because it really was such a terrifying time. And because the tickets were selling themselves, I didn’t have to worry about selling them. I focused my energy and our efforts on donations, fundraising and the community. Because at the beginning of the pandemic, I found myself in this position of ‘How do I help?’ I just couldn’t sit back and do nothing,” Sayegh recalled. Her creative efforts for the drive in included a 2020 showing of Willy Wonka and Chocolate Factory where golden tickets were hidden at local Cranford businesses and those that nabbed them earned free admission to the screening. Of course, amid the rise of streaming movies in the home coming out of the pandemic, followed by the 2023 Los Angeles writers and actors strikes, getting film lovers back into the Cranford Theater remained a challenge. “That was definitely a tough time, because our goal is to get people off their couches and into our seats to enjoy movies together on the big screen,” she remembered. To accomplish that, Sayegh knew the years of just opening the doors of a cinema and selling drinks and popcorn as people bought tickets were long past her industry. So she continued to think outside the box for new business opportunities. “That’s what we do here, try to create events around a lot of our films or classic films, and create ways for people to get excited and off their couches and into our theater to watch movies together and experience that together,” she explains of diversified programming like comedy shows, piano recitals, film festivals and indie film screenings. And just when that effort was paying dividends, Sayegh faced another major setback in April 2025 when part of the ceiling in her theater collapsed. Luckily, the building had few people in it at the time, and everyone was safely evacuated. “No one was hurt,” Sayegh recounted about that fateful night. “That was most important to me, because that would have changed the whole story. And the fact that no one was hurt meant I knew I was going to rebuild.” Doreen Sayegh renovated and reopened the Cranford Theater in Union County, New Jersey. Courtesy of Doreen Sayegh (2) After a seven-month closure, the now 99-year-old movie house reopened on Nov. 26, 2025 with marquee lights lit up and neon signage glowing. And among recent film offerings are movie shot locally as the Garden State enjoys a Hollywood production boom underpinned by film tax credits and other state incentives and local hires. Sayegh has shown New Jersey-shot pics like an advance screening for Steven Spielberg’s Disclosure Day , Steven Soderbergh’s supernatural thriller Presence, which was shot in Cranford, another thriller, Mother’s Instinct, starring Anne Hathway and Jessica Chastain, and Maybe I Do , featuring the late Diane Keaton and William H. Macy. “I love it when you have new visitors to our town, cast and crew coming in and they go out into our community and they grab a cup of coffee and a bite to eat,” she explains. Sayegh is also excited about upcoming Thanksgiving dates in her theater for another New Jersey-shot picture, Peter Farrelly’s I Play Rocky . That drama recounts the making of the 1976 Sylvester Stallone-starrer Rocky , a triumph-of-the-underdog saga that for Sayegh echoes the story of the Cranford Theater and recent efforts to keep the lights on the marquee lit up during the pandemic and a ceiling collapse. “The story of Rocky is so rooted in perseverance, resilience and continuing to fight when the odds are against you, and in many ways those themes resonate with the Cranford Theater’s own story and everything it has survived over the course of 100 years,” she said. Sayegh also puts her staying power down to her father’s influence, which instilled core values like honoring deals, treating people with respect and booking movies based on audience demand and not personal taste. And she looks forward to carrying on the legacy of a family-owned indie cinema business. “My father represents where it all started. I’m carrying that forward today, and now my five-year-old daughter, Natalia, is growing up in the theater much the same way I did. She is already watching and learning what it means to welcome people, take care of a theater and, most importantly, serve a community. I would love to see her running the show one day, although ultimately that will be her story to write,” Sayegh added. THR

title: ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone
full_text: Oct 3, 2026 1:17am PT ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone Shot before 'Heated Rivalry' launched its leading man to stardom, Michel K. Parandi's murky futuristic thriller will only be remembered — if at all — for that fortunate casting coup. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone 6 hours ago ‘Lady’ Review: Sian Clifford Lords It Over a Daffy English Class Satire 20 hours ago ‘Verity’ Review: Dakota Johnson and Anne Hathaway Drift Through Another Listless Colleen Hoover Adaptation 3 days ago See All Raindance Film Festival It would be nice to say that Connor Storrie burns up the screen in “ April X ,” the star’s first film vehicle released since TV’s “Heated Rivalry” made him hot property, but it would be overstating the case. Appropriating Harrison Ford’s “Blade Runner” frown, among a few other things nicked from that sci-fi classic in this sci-fi filler, Storrie capably shoulders a grim, po-faced tale of human cloning and trafficking in a greige dystopian future, but there’s not much for him to work with here — and he mostly projects the aura of a working actor dutifully waiting for something better to come along. Which it did, so job done. But you can hardly blame “April X” for riding his sudden celebrity, securing a theatrical release and escaping the straight-to-VOD morass that would appear to be its natural habitat. Related Stories Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Surely only Storrie’s most ardently committed new fans will venture out to see this, though: It’s hardly an embarrassing blot on his résumé, but it’ll be forgotten long before the second-season premiere of the queer hockey phenomenon. For writer-director Michel K. Parandi , making his feature-length debut, “April X” will be a more critical calling card — and duly shows off some resourceful technical ability on a cramped budget. But his script, co-written with regular collaborator Jack Coulter, is less impressive, welding together story scraps from other, better films to rather turbid, uninvolving effect. It occupies a similar genre space to the recent release “Hot Spot,” Agnieszka Smoczynska’s comparably scrappy, patched-together vision of compromised human identity in the middle-distance future; that film was a misfire, but a measure of its imaginative eccentricity would still be welcome here. Popular on Variety The year is unspecified, but the fatigued brutalist housing blocks of outer Bucharest are still standing: Though it doesn’t specify a location either, “April X” uses the present-day wear and tear of the Romanian capital, where the film was shot on location, as shorthand for a world collapsing into concrete ruin. The odd hi-tech drone adds some futuristic pizzazz to the film’s exterior vistas, but the new technologies defining the narrative aren’t of the gleaming, brave-new-world variety: People are being cloned in grubby, shadowed fashion, while memories and dreams can be captured and downloaded onto surprisingly retro-looking data devices. In this grimy waking nightmare, twins Baxter (Storrie) and April (German actor Lilly Krug) barely eke out a living doing a variety of sketchy jobs, some more criminal than others. He traffics organs on the black market, while she has a special gift for dreaming: At a time, apparently, when nobody has slumber visions anymore, hers are enviably lucid and vivid, to a marketable degree. April’s selling of her dreams to others wishing to experience her sensations isn’t a fresh idea — paging “Strange Days” — but it’s one of the more fertile ones here, and goes frustratingly unexploited as the film continues to probe a single glum reality. We’re more concerned with Baxter, whose underworld dealings eventually see him run afoul of local gangster Klein (Serban Pavlu), and the twins’ combined savings aren’t enough to allay the severe consequences. Soon April disappears, and Baxter’s desperate search for her begins. It’s ongoing when the story suddenly lurches five years into the future: The world looks much the same, but his hair is briefly longer, while April has seemingly been cloned into a number of identikit sex workers. Whether her brother can locate her soul in any one of them, or somehow implant it via her recorded memories, is the film’s big existential question — but the characters themselves aren’t drawn with enough warmth or personality for us to really care either way. Storrie soldiers through it all with a clenched jaw and a steely gaze, but the film’s world never comes fully to life. Nathan Haugaard’s sheeny widescreen lensing and Oana Novicov’s distressed production design ensure it looks pretty good, but “April X” is missing the granular particulars and textures that might make us believe it: The narrative, likewise, is just cohesive enough, but the details of Baxter’s life and livelihood are so muddy that he doesn’t have our full attention. Parandi’s film winds up outlining a dystopia more dull than devastating — though perhaps that’s the future we should really be fearing. ‘April X’ Review: Connor Storrie Bides His Time in a Generic Sci-Fi Clone Reviewed online, Oct. 2, 2026. title: DOJ Argues CNN & Other Outlets Can Be Banned From White House If Trump Determines They Didn’t Meet “Minimum Requirements Of Professionalism”
full_text: Skip to main content By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Kennedy Center Honors To Move To D.C.’s Capital One Arena Amid Closure Of Arts Complex U.S. Job Growth Slowed To 29,000 In September, With Slight Dip In Movie And Music Employment Fox News Tops September And Q3 Ratings; MS NOW Sees Gains, CNN Shows Uptick In Some Categories View All October 2, 2026 9:36pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Donald Trump Andrew Harnik/Getty Images The Justice Department argued that Donald Trump can legally ban CNN , MS NOW and Politico from the White House because he determined that they didn’t meet the “minimum requirements of professionalism.” Last month, a federal judge granted the three outlets a temporary restraining order that forced the White House to reinstate dozens of their reporters’ hard passes. The outlets are now asking the judge to extend that 14-day order for a longer term via a preliminary injunction, claiming that Trump’s ban is a violation of their First and Fifth amendment rights. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, has said that he is bound by the precedent set in In a 1977 D.C. Circuit opinion, Sherrill vs. Knight, in which the judges ruled that “the protection afforded newsgathering under the First Amendment guarantee of freedom of the press requires that this access not be denied arbitrarily or for less than compelling reasons.” Related Stories Late Night TV 'Real Time': Bill Maher Tells New Skydance Bosses "Don't Believe What Trump Is Tweeting About Me" News Kennedy Center Honors To Move To D.C.'s Capital One Arena Amid Closure Of Arts Complex In a court filing on Friday , the DOJ claimed that the Sherrill case still would allow for the president to restrict the three outlets from accessing the White House grounds because the White House has a “compelling interest.” Watch on Deadline The DOJ lawyers claimed that the Sherrill decision does not “prevent the President from concluding that bona fide journalists would identify sources instead of relying on anonymous sources, commit to factual accuracy, and provide the White House an opportunity to comment, rather than ‘perform their duties in a way that … interfere[s] with the White House’s daily operations.’ …At a bare minimum, it is a significant violation of decorum to publish classified and sensitive national security information.” The news outlets’ legal team has rejected that assertion, writing in a filing earlier this week that Trump’s “statements also make clear he implemented the ban to coerce more favorable coverage from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, and to deter other journalists and news organizations from newsgathering and reporting that the President might view as negative. And his administration has continued to retaliate against Plaintiffs even after the temporary restraining order, only underscoring that Defendants’ motive is to punish and chill journalism they dislike.” Even as access to the White House grounds has been reinstated, the White House has continued to restrict CNN from coverage of TV pool assignments, including travel with Trump on Air Force One. The outlets’ lawyers, led by Theodore Boutrous Jr., also noted that Trump and other White House officials “overlooked that the First Amendment protects reporting on matters affecting national security.” Kelly has set a hearing for Thursday on the news outlets’ motion for a preliminary injunction. In granting a TRO, Kelly concluded that the White House failed to provide due process to the news outlets. The DOJ has pointed to letters sent to the outlets as evidence that they were given due process. But those letters were sent on Sept. 22, four days after Trump’s ban was started. The judge also has noted that some of the objectionable stories cited by the DOJ do not have to do with national security. Kelly wrote in his order that “even the justifications provided to Plaintiffs after this case was filed are ambiguous about the true purpose of the revocations: while Defendants’ letters to Plaintiffs mention national security concerns, they purport to identify reporting that ‘threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods’ leaving open the possibility that all the stories fall into the later bucket, rather than the former.” Skydance Putting All 3 TV Studios Under George Cheeks: WBTV, CBS Studios, PTVS ‘Verity’ Solid $32M Start; ‘Digger’ At $10M Lowest Cruise Open In 19 Years What’s Next For De Luca, Abdy; Top Film Jobs To Greenstein, Goldberg Post-Merger Skydance Keeping Paramount+ & HBO Brands Read More About: 2 Comments

title: New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 2, 2026 8:00pm PT New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE) By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest New York’s Inaugural Muslim Film Festival Aims to Move Past Counter-Narratives, Unveils Lineup, Jury (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago Stray Kids Join BTS in Sitting Out Grammy Awards 1 day ago Oscars: Pakistan Selects Documentary ‘Hanging by a Wire’ for International Feature Race (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago See All New York Muslim Film Festival A festival launching Oct. 11 at Manhattan’s SVA Theatre is positioning itself as an answer to the flattened, stereotyped picture of Muslims Western media often traffics in. The New York Muslim Film Festival (NYMFF), billed as the city’s first for Muslim filmmakers, wants them telling their own stories. Hassan Babar, the festival’s artistic director, said such stories should not merely serve as counter-narratives. “They should be the establishing paradigm,” Babar said. Related Stories Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts The one-day event will screen 12 shorts from seven countries, with documentaries, dramas, comedies, animation and experimental pieces in the mix. Women make up a majority of the program’s directors. Popular on Variety “This festival exists because those stories deserve a stage in this city, not on the margins of someone else’s,” said Nawal Mubin, the festival’s co-founder and director. The day will open with a reception for filmmakers and industry guests. Two blocks of six films each, running roughly an hour apiece, will precede the awards and the jury announcement. Emmy winner Aasif Mandvi, a longtime “The Daily Show” correspondent who also starred in Paramount+ series “Evil,” sits on the six-member jury. He is joined by Arab-American writer-director Darine Hotait, founder of Cinephilia Productions, whose shorts have aired on HBO, AMC, SundanceTV and the BBC; Munir Atalla, head of production and acquisitions at Watermelon Pictures and a former Netflix creative executive; and producer Abubakar Khan, whose resume includes “The Glassworker,” Pakistan’s entry for the 2024 Oscars, and SXSW 2023 audience award winner “Mustache.” Rounding out the panel are Lebanese-American filmmaker Sarah Mokh, a Sundance Feature Film Fellow who recently wrapped her first feature, “The Alchemy of Being Okay,” which Khan is producing, and Egyptian-American actor Abubakr Ali. Ali has roles coming up in Bassam Tariq’s “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother,” opposite Mahershala Ali, and Sean Durkin’s A24 film “Deep Cuts,” and recently appeared in Kathryn Bigelow’s “A House of Dynamite.” Streamer Watermelon+ is behind the festival’s Watermelon+ Discovery Award. Its winner, whether filmmaker or rights holder, will give the platform an exclusive license to show the film for a limited period. The Islamic Scholarship Fund, New York production and post house Lost in Space, and Aneesa Talks, which filmmaker Aneesa Khan founded to support South Asian and Muslim creatives, have also signed on as partners. The program ranges widely in tone and subject. Justin Mashouf’s documentary “$17.74” follows a former gang member, behind bars since the 1980s, whose gesture of support for Gaza from inside prison set off a viral wave of solidarity. In Karim Emara’s Qatar-U.S. dramedy “Baba Is Melting,” a son phones his father, who is waiting in the car before Friday prayer in Doha, to challenge him over a hidden second marriage. Zaid Ahmed Hassan’s “Ghusl” centers on a son whose dying father asks him to learn Islamic burial rites, while Basma Khalifa’s U.K. experimental piece “Henna” follows the henna plant’s life cycle alongside women from 16 African and SWANA countries. Sima Naseem’s Canada-Pakistan animation “My Friend in the Jingle Truck” combines stop-motion and 2D to tell of a Karachi girl who meets a magical bird. In Alex Aljouni’s “Bukra,” a young Syrian refugee whose sweepstakes prize is a soccer ball rushes to collect it in time for one last match with her best friend before he is gone for good. One daring move reopens old rifts among three generations of Afghan women in Negine Jasmine Sekandari and Ayda Rojhantalab’s comedy “Haram Salami,” as they weigh who they are against what custom demands and what they want. Maram Taibah’s Saudi fantasy “Malika” explores a girl’s bond with her grandmother, and the pull between wildness and the obedience expected of girls, through a magical-realist world spun from a child’s imagination. In Bilal Shams Khan’s Pakistani drama “Sabr O Shukar,” 10-year-old Akram learns about patience and gratitude while chasing his dream of a bicycle. Imran J. Khan’s “The Boy With Dinosaur Head” pits a troubled boy who believes he is a dinosaur against a teacher set on pulling him back to reality, and their short encounter stays with both of them. Ilhan Abdullahi and Sherry Rashidan’s Canadian comedy “Unqualified” follows Warsan, the lone Muslim at her workplace, who is handed the job of spiritually cleansing a lunchroom said to be haunted and must clear out the spirits, armed with her faith and a string of misunderstandings, before she loses her job. Lyna Tadount and Sofian Chouaib’s French drama “Ya Hanouni” centers on two parents vying to be their baby’s first word, until their lighthearted contest is cut short by an event that upends their lives. Babar, a Toronto-based actor and producer, co-heads programming with Aneesa Khan, who also leads communications. Mubin, a New York director-producer, co-founded the festival with filmmaker and post-production specialist Giuseppe de Matteis. Both work at Lost in Space. title: Pedro Pascal Was Surprised Tony Gilroy Made ‘Behemoth!’ “So Intimate And Healing”: “I Thought You Were Gonna Be Mean”
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Zach Bryan Dons “Free Palestine” Shirt For Concert At Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium Pedro Pascal Was Surprised Tony Gilroy Made ‘Behemoth!’ “So Intimate And Healing”: “I Thought You Were Gonna Be Mean” ‘Real Time’: Bill Maher Tells New Skydance Bosses “Don’t Believe What Trump Is Tweeting About Me” View All October 2, 2026 7:53pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Pedro Pascal in 'Behemoth!' (2026) Justin Lubin/Searchlight Productions/Courtesy Everett Collection With the world premiere of Behemoth! , Pedro Pascal is praising Tony Gilroy for the intimate drama. During a Q&A after the film’s premiere screening at the New York Film Festival, the Golden Globe-nominated actor admitted he thought Gilroy was “gonna be kinda mean” before they worked together. “You have created this complex Jason Bourne-like puzzle over something that is so intimate and so healing this mysterious way,” Pascal told Gilroy in a video shared by NYFF . “And I didn’t think it was gonna come from him, you know what I mean? This intimidating intellectual … you know, I thought you were gonna be kinda mean. And you thought I was gonna be a dork. title: “Good Heavens”: Kathleen Turner Reacts to Michael Douglas’ Bombshell About Their Secret Romance During ‘Romancing the Stone’
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 2, 2026 6:21pm Kathleen Turner and Michael Douglas. Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images for AFI Michael Douglas revealed in a new excerpt from his memoir One Helluva Ride that he and Kathleen Turner had a secret romantic relationship while filming 1984’s Romancing the Stone , and the actress is responding to his revelation. The Fatal Attraction actor shared an exclusive excerpt from his new memoir with People Thursday, writing that he and his then-wife, Diandra Douglas, were separated and “were both having extramarital affairs.” He wrote that “Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship,” and vowed to keep their romance private. Related Stories Movies Michael Douglas, Willem Dafoe Reunite with Oliver Stone for Drama 'White Lies' Movies 'Basic Instinct' Writer Joe Eszterhas to Pen Reboot Movie for Amazon MGM Studios “The chemistry I had with Kathleen Turner was so strong, audiences have been certain for years that we were in a relationship together while making the film. We both denied it through Romancing The Stone, Jewel of the Nile, War of the Roses , and even while doing press a few years ago for The Kominsky Method ,” he said, noting four projects they’ve worked on together. “The official story went as follows: Yes, we confessed, we had amazing chemistry. Yes, we were both, as Kathleen said, ‘terrible flirts,’ and yes, we were both tempted, but nothing ever happened between us,” Douglas wrote, per the excerpt. “That was a lie.” Turner responded to Douglas’ admission on Friday. “Good heavens what a fuss about something 40 years ago!” the actress wrote in a statement shared with People . “I love Michael and I look forward to enjoying the book.” Elsewhere in his excerpt, the two-time Oscar winner said they lied about their romance for 40 years “to protect my wife and son.” He said they kept things so under wraps that director Bob Zemeckis and their co-star Danny DeVito “were unaware.” “The truth is that during the production of Romancing the Stone , Kathleen and I fell hard for each other and began a relationship,” Douglas wrote. “It wasn’t a fly-by night affair; it grew naturally from how closely we were working together, how much pressure we were under, how much we respected and cared for one another, and how attracted we were to each other. Like every other guy in the world at the time, I was knocked sideways by Kathleen….” Douglas wrote that during a set visit, Diandra “grew suspicious,” and spoke with Turner and “made it clear to her that we were still married.” “Her view of the terms of our separation was different from mine. This gave Kathleen pause. She didn’t want to interfere,” he wrote. “After that visit, Kathleen and I ended things, and I went back to Diandra.” THR

title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama
full_text: Oct 2, 2026 5:00pm PT ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama It understands the classical-music world and has fun fiddling around with film form. But is that enough? By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: Paul Thomas Anderson Directs a Rapturous Solo Concert Movie Built Around the Songs — and Haunting Sound — of Cameron Winter 1 day ago Robert Pattinson Is a New Kind of Movie Star: The Anti-Tom Cruise 3 days ago ‘Digger’ Review: As a Texas Oil Tycoon, Tom Cruise Goes Over the Top in Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Bombastically Self-Important Satire 4 days ago See All Courtesy of Searchlight Pictures I was a classical musician growing up, so I’m probably more disposed than most to like a movie set in the classical-music world. Then again, that could mean that I set a higher bar for authenticity when it comes to depicting it. There’s no doubt that the cinema’s reigning masterpiece of classical-music drama is “Tár” — a great movie in so many other ways that that remains only one dimension of it. But Todd Field inhabited that world, and allowed the audience to do so, in a way that no previous director had. Two other films leap to mind that have the ring of deep-dish classical-music reality: “Mr. Holland’s Opus,” which beautifully caught the experience of studying music in high school, and “Maestro,” a movie I may have enjoyed more than others, even though it left out a ton of stuff about Leonard Bernstein (like, for instance, the heart of his conducting career in the ’50s and ’60s!), because I instinctively filled all of that in. Related Stories Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Viewed on that scale, “ Behemoth! ,” Tony Gilroy ’s drama about a professional cellist, played with perky mystery by Pedro Pascal , scores on the level of authenticity. Pascal’s character, a renowned musician named Alex Serian, has been a member of various world-class symphony orchestras, notably in Chicago, but the film presents us with a more plugged-in contempo angle on this kind of career. In the new era, orchestras are foundering, the pay isn’t what it used to be, and even a virtuoso string musician might need a side gig or two. For Alex, that has meant playing in orchestras that are assembled to record movie scores — a major industry, and one that “Behemoth!” depicts as being nearly as high maintenance as the prestige symphony circuit. Popular on Variety The conductors who oversee the recording of the movie scores are portrayed as hyper-demanding corporate perfectionists. (One of them, a prima donna played by Thomas Kretschmann, makes it feel like you’re seeing Klaus Kinski going to work for Skydance.) And from the film’s opening scene, which immerses us in the lingo of rehearsal, which is a mixture of old-school classical Euro directives (“pianissimo”) and Hollywood jargon (“new ink”), we’re right there in the cavernous recording studio, feeling the heat and the nuance. My all-time pet peeve in classical-music films is that characters who are supposed to be playing the violin or cello almost never look real — you can see from a mile away that they’re faking it, imitating the finger and bow movements like crude mimes. Tony Gilroy has solved this problem in the most committed way possible: He had Pedro Pascal learn to play the cello. That’s really Pascal doing it, which is why everything about his motions looks real, from the vibrato to the bowing to the way he moves his head. That devotion works for the film. It allows us to feel that Alex is as genuine in his talent as a professional athlete or a star chef. Virtuosity is the air he breathes. Not every orchestra player is a virtuoso, of course, but Alex, we learn, was a child prodigy who came from a high-powered musical family (we see a clip of him playing Bach as a 6-year-old on “The Tonight Show”). That’s his pedigree, and it’s also his problem, since the family craziness has messed him up. In addition to presenting its musical demimonde with reverent accuracy, “Behemoth!” has another quality going for it: The film is playful. It’s not a symphony — it’s a scherzo. This is only the fourth feature Gilroy has directed (it’s his first since “The Bourne Legacy” in 2012), but coming off the “Star Wars” television series “Andor,” which he created and was the showrunner for, he makes his enthusiasm for the filmmaking process palpable. For most of the film, Alex is doing movie-score session work, and Gilroy introduces an impish device: We see and hear the orchestra recording a score (the music might be suspenseful, romantic, pensive), until seconds later it becomes the score of “Behemoth!” itself. I’m not honestly sure I can say what this slightly meta gambit accomplishes, but it’s clever and fun. Gilroy got no less than nine acclaimed film composers to contribute their talents to the movie (they include James Newton Howard and Alan Silvestri and are billed as the Behemoth! Collective). But he could easily have executed the exact same trick with just one composer. Leaping around in time, Gilroy draws us into Alex’s world with an effervescent wink at the badness of his behavior. Alex is wriggling out of a fling with Carol, the wife of one of the Chicago orchestra’s wealthy patrons — she’s played by Olivia Wilde, who radiates such intense stalker energy here that we’re not quite sure how to react. Alex just keeps calm, and that’s what Pascal does, more or less, throughout the movie. Alex’s life is falling apart, yet somehow he’s the eye of the storm; everyone around him is screwier than he is. With an elegant mustache and perfect gelled hair that dips down onto his forehead, Pedro Pascal has never looked more dashing — he’s like a refined Burt Reynolds, or maybe a passive Brando. Between his classical chops and his glamorous looks, women drop for Alex, but he’s an artist who has drifted through life, drinking and having flings, always ready to move on to the next woman and the next city and the next gig. It’s a frictionless life he revels in. But something’s got to give. Gilroy seems to have been influenced by the elliptical quality of “Tár,” though not always to good effect. I enjoyed, to a point, the cut-and-paste chronology of “Behemoth!,” but there’s a flaw in it: The actors look identical in every scene, so some of it is confusing — like the episode in Dallas where Alex meets Nadia (Eva Victor), a star violinist who seems his match. They sleep together. But then, after a fraught phone conversation with the billionaire who wants to marry her, she lashes out at Alex (who has done nothing wrong), and we’re not sure where this is going or why. A few scenes later, tragedy has struck. But did all these events happen one after another or years apart? We figure it out, but Gilroy should have made it easier to read. Alex, after the debacle of his break-up with Wilde’s clingy diva in Chicago, returns to Los Angeles, where he grew up. He can get session work there, and does. He still seems mellow, but he’s bestirred by a pet obsession: listening to the original avant-pop compositions posted online by Viviana ( Alexa Swinton ), a 15-year-old girl who has become a local celebrity. It turns out that he’s got a connection to her; she’s Nadia’s daughter. But why is he so interested? He’s just got…a feeling. Alex’s brother, a talented but scruffy podcast host, is played by Will Arnett with a lived-in self-doubt more interesting than anything about his character in “Is This Thing On?” It’s through their conversations that we start to piece together Alex’s troubled family life — but here, once again, Pascal suffers in such a placid way that we keep wanting more. The movie finally comes to a head in an expertly staged suspense sequence where Alex, pretending to be a caterer’s assistant, sneaks into Nadia’s stone mansion, finds what he was looking for, and then has to sneak out. Naturally, the music playing under all this is “movie music.” What, in the end, is “Behemoth!,” apart from a movie with a dismally bad title? (You can’t remember it. You can’t pronounce it. And it’s hard to say what, exactly, it means or why it carries an exclamation point — though it is, of course, the title of one of the films that Alex is helping to record the score for.) “Behemoth!” is a midlife-crisis movie. It’s a classical-musician movie. It’s a mild romantic mystery. It’s Tony Gilroy fiddling around with pure movie form. (He’s a sly orchestrator of big-screen storytelling.) But 19 years after “Michael Clayton,” he’s still looking for a subject that will allow him to do what he did so masterfully in that movie: heighten our perceptions of the world along with our emotions, until they become one. ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Is a Classical Cellist Skating Through a Midlife Crisis in Tony Gilroy’s Elevated Bauble of a Music Drama Reviewed at Dolby 88 (New York Film Festival, Centerpiece), Oct. 1, 2026.
