title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Hints at Soulful Depths, but the Drama Keeps Stalling in Tony Gilroy’s Wan Character Study of a Virtuoso Cellist
full_text: Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All October 2, 2026 5:00pm Pedro Pascal in 'Behemoth!' Justin Lubin/Searchlight Pictures Tony Gilroy returns to features after 14 years’ absence — the last three of them spent in the Star Wars TV trenches as creator, showrunner and head writer on Andor — with a movie that makes itself hard to love. Hampered by a fussy hopscotching time structure that too often halts the dramatic momentum and by a central character whose passivity fights against the warmth and magnetism of Pedro Pascal in the role, Behemoth! is an odd duck, alternately intriguing and frustrating. What it does have going for it is a series of thrilling sequences observing the workings of an orchestra employed on Hollywood’s scoring stages. Related Stories Movies 'Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall' Review: Paul Thomas Anderson's Effectively Austere Concert Doc Puts You Right in the Room Movies Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes Documentary Holds a Raucous and Revealing NYFF Screening That rarely glimpsed milieu and a virtuoso cellist protagonist might make Gilroy’s film sound like Maestro meets Tár . But the story’s internal engine seldom revs hard enough to stand up to either of those comparisons, despite its capable ensemble cast and polished craftsmanship. Behemoth! The Bottom Line Adagio when it needs to be agitato. Venue : New York Film Festival (Centerpiece — Main Slate) Release date : Friday, Dec. 4 Cast : Pedro Pascal, Olivia Wilde, Eva Victor, Alexa Swinton, Kaya Ralls, Erik Griffin, JoBeth Williams, Margarita Levieva, Hank Azaria, Will Arnett Director-screenwriter : Tony Gilroy 2 hours 7 minutes One issue is that the script by Gilroy (an Oscar nominee for screenwriting and direction on Michael Clayton ) gives insufficient dimension to Pascal’s character, Alex Serian, for someone meant to carry a film. He’s a sideliner in his own life, which may well be the result of living in the shadow of a family of narcissists, but that is not enough to make him interesting. Nor does it help that Alex’s failed relationships seem less a symptom of his own damage than his poor choice of partners. The women characters generally are not drawn kindly, especially Carol Spedding ( Olivia Wilde ), a wealthy, married arts patron whose ferocious pursuit of Alex when he ends their affair makes her seem like a soul sister to Glenn Close in Fatal Attraction . Maybe Carol’s $6 million gift to the Chicago Symphony during Alex’s tenure there enables her to feel some kind of ownership, though that’s more implied than explored. “I bleed for you and you shun me?” screeches the manic drama queen after he blocks her calls. Alex’s flight from scary Carol lands him back in his hometown, Los Angeles, after 20 years of playing in other cities, looking to get back into session work recording orchestral film scores. It’s in those scenes on studio lots — including the Barbra Streisand Scoring Studio at Sony — that the movie is most dynamic. That’s in large part due to the staggering range of ravishing original film music we see being performed — from dark drama to suspense to action to soaring romance — written by an assembly of nine respected composers billed as “The Behemoth! Collective.” They include Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandan Roberts and Alan Silvestri. Much of their work also plays over scenes elsewhere in the movie, including an art rock song, a requiem, a cartoon theme tune, a harp concerto and cello etudes. For anyone who loves movies, being prompted to think about the experiential role that a great score plays is fascinating, but while Behemoth! feints toward being a celebration of film music, it never fully commits. It seems a missed opportunity that we don’t get to watch music being matched to specific beats on the screen, beyond background shots of fuzzy footage on a monitor. Alex’s relationship with his parents was defined by their need to outshine their children. We see video of Alex playing Bach at age 6 on Johnny Carson’s show, but the film seems to suggest their nurturing of their sons’ musical gifts was just another way to burnish their own reputations. His self-absorbed brother Andy ( Will Arnett , who’s in a different movie) became something of a black sheep when he turned his back on classical viola to form a briefly successful rock band in the ‘90s. He now hosts a podcast about the TV and movie themes of their late father Peter ( Hank Azaria , in a video cameo). Their mother Ginnie (an unrecognizable JoBeth Williams ) was a renowned harpist, fading fast with dementia when Alex stays with her upon first returning to L.A. She once said of her husband, “He was a Peter who really wanted to be a Pierre.” But those glimmers of insight fail to coalesce into a fleshed-out family mythology — though we do learn that Alex and Andy’s grandfather died from a stroke, immedicately after hitting a high C while playing trumpet on the same MGM stage where Alex now works. There’s simply not enough meat on the bones of the parental background or in Alex and Andy’s conversations about them to give much shape to the supposedly chaotic upbringing that formed them. The movie is more engaged in Alex’s reflections on his own life in the two decades since he left, jumping between fizzled relationships and elite orchestra positions in Boston, Dallas and Chicago. The one woman he appears to have loved is brilliant violinist Nadia ( Eva Victor ), who bailed to marry a billionaire businessman (Matthew Lillard). Victor ( Sorry, Baby ) is a vivid screen presence, but Nadia isn’t around long enough to leave much of an impression before Alex’s memories jump to her funeral six years later. It’s on that solemn occasion that he first sees Nadia’s prodigiously gifted daughter Viviana when she plays an original piano composition of astonishing maturity. That piques Alex’s curiosity about the possibility that he might be the girl’s father; his paternity sleuthing gives the movie a much-needed kick. While Alex’s romantic past is too thinly outlined to be compelling, Pascal’s internalized performance becomes more affecting once the character’s paternal instincts emerge. This happens first with Bronte (Kaya Ralls), a bright young cellist he coaches for an audition with the prestigious San Francisco Symphony. (Professional musician Ralls is a natural in her first acting role.) But it’s when he starts following Viviana’s success as a composer and musician across multiple genres that the film finally gains some emotional heft. An interlude during which their professional paths cross, when 15-year-old Viviana (Alexa Swinton, terrific) is hired to take over scoring duties on a major movie from a temperamental Euro-diva (Thomas Kretschmann, amusingly playing a male Lydia Tár), is lovely. But it comes too late in a movie that gives us few reasons to care about its opaque central character. Behemoth! is handsomely shot by Damián García, who previously worked with Gilroy on Andor , but in the end it’s satisfying only as a sensory experience in which music acquires physical form, an aspect greatly enhanced by the advanced sound technology of Dolby Atmos. title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Hits All The Right Notes In Tony Gilroy’s Lyrical Love Letter To The Music Of The Movies – New York Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Pete Hammond Pete Hammond Awards Columnist/Chief Film Critic @DeadlinePete More Stories By Pete Kevin Feige Accepts Will Rogers Foundation Pioneer Of The Year, Promises Many More Movies To Come ‘Verity’ Review: Dakota Johnson And Anne Hathaway Play Authors In Psychological Thriller, But Are They Really Alter Egos For Colleen Hoover? ‘Digger’ Review: Tom Cruise Explodes In Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Surprising And Urgent Disaster Movie Satire View All October 2, 2026 5:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Behemoth!' Searchlight It has been 14 years since Tony Gilroy last directed a feature film, 2012’s The Bourne Legacy. Before that was Duplicity and in 2007 his sensational Oscar-nominated Michael Clayton. He has been busy though, notably the critically acclaimed TV series Andor, but it is good to see his rare sophisticated storytelling back on the big screen with the compelling journey of a lifelong cellist whose nomad-like life reaches a crescendo and turning point after years of following the music professionally and personally. Behemoth! , which had its world premiere today at the New York Film Festival , is the rare movie set in the world of Hollywood music soundstages and it undoubtedly is a love letter to this crucial, usually final, aspect of the production process. But its central focus is on the family and romantic ties of one musician, Alex Serian ( Pedro Pascal ), who was born to be in an orchestra — in fact he couldn’t escape it — and that has taken its toll on this man for whom music is the one and only steady beat in his life, if not his heart. Related Stories Documentary ‘You Can See Everything’ Directors On Filming Complex Doc: “If We Can’t Agree On What’s Happening, There’s Something There” – NYFF Festivals NYFF Turns Up The Heat As ‘Godzilla’, ‘Artificial’, ‘NAZA’, ‘You Can See Everything’ Spark Festival Buzz Alex’s grandfather was a session musician for movies who died playing on one in 1959; his absent father, Peter ( Hank Azaria ), also was a composer for cartoons and television, if not a creatively satisfied one; his mother Ginnie ( Jo Beth Williams ) was a successful musician herself; as was his brother Andy ( Will Arnett ), who had a taste of fame in a ’90s rock band. In many ways the devotion to their professional life all took a toll on this family, and in Alex’s case turned him inward — a traveling cello player drifting from city to city, and relationship to relationship, being on the road the only real life he knew, his true potential never completely met. Watch on Deadline Now after 20 years he is returning to Los Angeles, getting day work on a number of movie-scoring sessions but also dealing with family issues including the failing health of his mother, his brother’s quirkiness, and perhaps the biggest lingering question he has still in his life via an encounter with a 15- year-old prodigy, Viviana Glenn (Alexa Swinton), who not only has a huge following on the pop circuit (think Billie Eilish) but who also has now been called in to replace the composer on the movie Behemoth! (a code name for the secret film the are working on). All of this is played out in non-linear fashion as we meet Alex on a session for a movie, but as he plays the notes, Gilroy’s script goes to flashbacks of his earlier life, back and forth between present day and various years, jobs and romantic liaisons. First we get a look at his past romantic entanglements as one woman yells at him complaining about another she discovers he slept with. That one is a funny bit with a determined Carol Spedding ( Olivia Wilde ), with whom Alex had a fling in Chicago, but is now taking things overboard insisting he made a huge mistake breaking it off. This woman is just one boiling bunny removed from a restraining order and Wilde amusingly plays it for all its worth. In another flashback in Dallas we meet fellow musician Nadia Hynes ( Eva Victor ), who is involved sexually with the emotionally reserved Alex while at the same time committed to another very wealthy man, Dennis Glenn (Matthew Lillard). Cutting to six years later she has tragically died and Alex finds himself invited to her funeral, where her very young daughter Viviana demonstrates her unique talents with a piano composition. Alex begins to get a nagging feeling this girl could actually be his daughter from that long-ago relationship. Her musical abilities are just one clue. While at the funeral he runs into an old flame and close friend of Nadia (Margarita Levieva), leading both again to the bedroom. It won’t be the last time he visits this mansion as his quest for the truth leads him back in a totally different guise. Gilroy skillfully weaves all these vignettes in and out, each with its own particular musical theme as again it is music always leading the way through the maze of Alex Serian’s life. To do this no single composer was hired to create the all-important score, but rather nine well-known maestros with distinct talents — Michael Giacchino, James Newton Howard, Michael Abels, Emily Bear, Lukas Frank, Henry Jackman, Nami Melumad, Brandon Roberts and Alan Silvestri — who together make up The Behemoth! Collective, and who serve up a musical score that, to my ears, is hands down the year’s best. The memorable original song written for the fictional Viviana, “Your God Is Sleeping,” could be a major hit. Combined with magnificent sound design, Behemoth! is a feast for the ears. A total of 303 AFM musicians in Los Angeles were used in the musical sequences. And for all the talk of L.A.’s sad production decline as a shooting location, Gilroy has delivered a winning antidote for that as the City Of Angels has never looked so good. Pascal, utterly convincing as this accomplished musician, subtly plays Alex in a low-key style with no showboating or anything that rings false in a portrayal where he simply becomes this wandering soul in search of himself after years of denial. The supporting players (Carmen Cuba was casting director) could not be better. Victor ( Sorry, Baby ) is quite good as Nadia, nailing the complicated feelings of someone married to her music like Alex but confused in love. Kaya Ralls is a complete delight as Bronte, a young fellow musician Alex mentors; Swinton as the 15 year old Viviana is superb; Williams is equally impressive as Alex’s mother in two poignant scenes 10 years apart; Azaria as Alex’s dad is terrific, seen via a brutally honest video letter Alex discovers 25 years after it was recorded; and Wilde and Arnett are in for lighter moments that offer a nice balance to the heavier ones. Erik Griffin also has some good moments as the orchestra manager. In the end though, Behemoth! is not just a revealing character study of a man ultimately looking for his true place in the world, but also a gorgeous and glorious tribute to those who make the music that help make movies like this one so much richer. Producers are Gilroy, Sanne Wohlenberg and John Gilroy (who also did the complex editing for the film). Title: Behemoth! title: George Cheeks May Be Poised for Expanded TV Role at Skydance Post Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger

Merge 2 days ago See All CBS Paramount TV media chair George Cheeks , whose domain has included all of CBS in addition to the Paramount cable networks, is said to be in line for an expanded oversight at the newly merged Paramount-Warner Bros. entity (which will be named “ Skydance ,” the company revealed Friday). Skydance would not comment, but Cheeks has been seen as a strong lieutenant overseeing the TV properties under Paramount ever since Skydance took control of the company last August. Prior to that, Cheeks was one of the three co-CEOs of Paramount Global — and was the only one of that triumvirate to make the transition to the new company. Related Stories Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Speculation and rumors of how the structure on the TV network and studio side might play out have been heavy over the past few days, now that the question of how the streaming structure at the merged company has been settled (with HBO boss Casey Bloys on top and Paramount direct-to-consumer head Cindy Holland exiting). Popular on Variety Many of the questions in the more traditional Hollywood world of TV networks and studios — still a hefty revenue driver — have centered on what roles Skydance head David Ellison might have in mind for Warner Bros. TV Group and WBD U.S. Networks chairman/CEO Channing Dungey and Cheeks. Both execs are well-liked and respected, and both boast tremendous domains, consisting of both studios and networks. One scenario making the rounds has Cheeks potentially overseeing all of the vast TV holdings of the combined company, but so far, there’s no firm confirmation and a final structure isn’t expected to be announced until next week. All eyes will also be on what role Ellison picks for Dungey, whose tenure at Warner Bros. TV Group continues to be extremely successful . Under Dungey, the studio produces more than 80 original series for more than 20 platforms, including HBO, HBO Max and others, with series like “Ted Lasso,” “Abbott Elementary”, “The Bachelor” franchise, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage,” “The Jennifer Hudson Show,” “The Pitt,” “Running Point,” “Shrinking,” “Rooster,” “The Voice” and the upcoming “Harry Potter” series. So far this year, the division has landed 13 new series orders and 13 series renewals, while “The Pitt” just landed six Emmys — including its second for outstanding drama. Dungey also took on oversight of WBD’s U.S. Networks in 2025, including Discovery Channel, Food Network, HGTV, Investigation Discovery, TLC, Adult Swim, Animal Planet, Cartoon Network, Cooking Channel, HLN, OWN, Science Channel, TBS, TNT, Travel Channel, Tru TV and Turner Classic Movies. When Variety spoke to Dungey last month, she said she had met with Ellison in more of a “getting to know you” setting. Beyond that, she expressed her desire to stick with the company post-merger: “I love my team at Warner Bros. Television Group. I love our shows, our talent. And I’ve become very happy in my U.S. networks role, which was something that I didn’t see coming almost two years ago. The best-case scenario for me is something that allows me to continue to play around in both of these spaces.” Among the possible setups that observers have spitballed was the idea of splitting their oversight between networks and studios. But if Cheeks does take control of the entire TV business, the biggest question will be whether Dungey will opt to remain and report to him. Insiders say the two have a good rapport, particularly as Warner Bros. TV has been a hefty supplier of series to CBS over the years — including the successful crop of Chuck Lorre comedies that have aired on the Eye. Beyond that, the question also remains as to how Warner Bros. TV (run by president Brett Paul and creative affairs president Clancy Collins White), CBS Studios (run by president David Stapf), and Paramount TV Studios (run by Matt Thunell) will all be integrated. CBS Studios is also a major enterprise, producing more than 60 series, while Paramount TV Studios has a hefty slate including the Taylor Sheridan shows. Currently, Stapf and Thunell report to Cheeks, while Paul and Collins White report to Dungey. There could be a scenario where Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios and Paramount TV Studios continue as separate labels. Cheeks had previously been president and CEO of CBS, having joined Paramount in March 2020. This repped his second stint there, having first joined MTV Networks (a part of the then-Viacom company) in 1998 and later taking on roles including exec VP of business affairs and general counsel for the Viacom Music and Entertainment Groups. Cheeks later moved to NBC in 2012 as president of business operations and late-night programming, then became co-chairman of NBC Entertainment and later as vice chairman of NBCUniversal Content Studios. Deadline was first to report of Cheeks’ potential new role at Skydance. title: ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion)
full_text: Oct 2, 2026 4:15pm PT ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion) By William Earl Plus Icon William Earl @beautifulbill Latest ‘Digger’: How Its Big Twist Saves the Movie From Being a Complete Disaster (Opinion) 15 hours ago Chris Hansen Confronts ‘Primetime’: The Tragic Ending, Seeing His Love Life Onscreen and Considering Legal Action Against A24 Because ‘They Exploited Me’ 2 days ago Variety and Outfront Announce Experience and Culture Summit: The IRL Advantage, Featuring Questlove, Charlamagne tha God and Ice-T 4 days ago See All ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection SPOILER ALERT: This story contains major spoilers for “ Digger ,” in theaters now via Warner Bros. When does a bad movie become a fascinating watch? So often the kiss of death for a feature is boredom; that feeling you’ve seen the same story many times before, the actors are checked out, there’s no visual panache. That’s not the case with “Digger.” While it’s shaping up to be a box office disaster , the movie is anything but dull. Tom Cruise leads the cast in acting to the rafters, DP Emmanuel Lubezki keeps the camera moving and director Alejandro G. Iñárritu injects plenty of swagger in the proceedings. Related Stories Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Unfortunately, the film’s opening — an extended introduction to Cruise’s ambitious oilman Digger Rockwell — is so in-your-face that it sags under the weight. Cruise is in grotesque prosthetics, eager to show us as quickly as possible how uncouth Digger is: He eats from the same can of sardines as his beloved cat, his butt crack is seen in plain view of his maid, his comb-over wisps wildly. Popular on Variety It’s a clichéd character surrounded by other bobbling caricatures that enter and exit the rooms of his mansion, flailing wildly as Digger learns that his oil company might have inadvertently caused a climate-based global disaster. It’s shrill and tired, and despite the best intentions of the filmmakers to cause provocation around environmentalism, it’s about as subtle as Cruise turning to the camera and screaming, “DO YOU GET IT?!?” Ultimately, the poster’s promise of “a comedy of catastrophic proportions” seems more like a threat than a guarantee of “Dr. Strangelove”-esque genius. But then, an interesting twist happens. No, “Digger” isn’t a musical , but rather reveals that everything we’ve seen so far is a group of actors rehearsing an ambitious play about Digger called “Fossil Fools.” We’re witnessing the tech rehearsal hours before the show is set to debut in front of an audience, and Cruise drops his broad southern accent, revealing himself as Curtis Markson, the star of the show who has difficulty finding the satirical rhythm. It’s an engagingly meta turn, and shows much more of Cruise’s psyche than audiences might expect. During a teflon press tour hyping “Digger,” journalists weren’t able to conjure anything personal or interesting from him. But during a scene where Cruise argues with “Fossil Fools” director Hannah (Sophie Wilde) about satire versus real-world events, the artifice of Cruise’s fat suit and cowboy boots melts away, and the fire in his eyes that made iconic performances in films like “Magnolia” and “Eyes Wide Shut” blaze returns in flashes. It also helps to contextualize Iñárritu’s vision of satire itself. Some reviews of “Digger” have knocked the very idea of satirical films in 2026. After all, how can anything feel larger-than-life in the Trump era? But given the put-on-a-show staging, the film’s structure adds further firepower to standout scenes like Digger holding court in the United Nations, tap-dancing around a global community ready to feed him to the wolves after he doubles down on his wrongdoing. The showcase scene is emphasized by the fact that everything is underwritten by Digger’s real-life nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), who bought the rights to “Fossil Fools” and used his vast wealth to fund the production. His motivations are many, as he implies that he’s doing it out of a mix of penance, flagellation and tribute to his family name. But ultimately he’s a benefactor of the arts. The themes make it impossible to ignore the real-life soap opera currently happening at “Digger” studio Warner Bros., where new owner David Ellison swears he bought the company for all the right reasons . “Digger” ends on a somber note, with the audience methodically putting on gas masks and emptying the gorgeous theater, stepping into the dystopian world that remains after Digger’s environmental disaster. Flooded streets, discarded cars and military police are all around, until the camera tilts to the sky and the soundtrack becomes overwhelmed with the natural noises of wild animals. It’s a chilling wrap, as well as a dour end to what appears to be the last Warner Bros. film ever released . Not all of the elements tied to the twist work — Curtis’ search for his daughter’s missing flight during the tech rehearsal is curiously underbaked — but at least it teases a flurry of ideas instead of drowning in clumsy dialogue. At its best, it recalls Charlie Kaufman’s far superior 2008 film “Synecdoche, New York,” in which Philip Seymour Hoffman is a theater director who, in the pursuit of truth, creates a full-scale recreation of New York City in a warehouse in order to accurately reflect life. It, too, looks at the idea of understanding larger truths through a stage production, but is more clever and sincere. Ultimately, even the decision to add another layer, becoming a story about art just as much as one about the climate crisis, doesn’t escalate “Digger” into must-see territory. But the cross section of cinephiles who will be compelled to catch it in theaters — Cruise completists, flop aficionados, rubberneckers who want to see the world burn — will have more to chew on than the artifice presented at the beginning. title: Selma Blair Announces ‘Hineni’ Doc About Antisemitism After She Was “Erased” Over Islamophobic Comments
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Zach Bryan Dons “Free Palestine” Shirt For Concert At Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium Pedro Pascal Was Surprised Tony Gilroy Made ‘Behemoth!’ “So Intimate And Healing”: “I Thought You Were Gonna Be Mean” ‘Real Time’: Bill Maher Tells New Skydance Bosses “Don’t Believe What Trump Is Tweeting About Me” View All October 2, 2026 4:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Selma Blair attends Variety Power of Women LA on Sept. 23, 2026 in Beverly Hills, California. River Callaway/PMC More than two years later, Selma Blair is taking the fallout over her Islamophobic comments and channeling it into a documentary about antisemitism . On Thursday, the actress announced at the ADL State of the Arts Reception in New York City that she’s making a documentary entitled Hineni ( Here I Am ) to say what she “couldn’t say two years ago” when she first apologized for her comments . “Two years ago I learned what erased feels like, and I’ve decided the opposite of erased is making something. So I’m making a film,” she said in her remarks . “The last time I let cameras in, it was about my body. This time it’s about my people. It’s a documentary about antisemitism, and as confounding and confusing as it seems to be because no one wants to talk about geopolitics but it seems to get intermingled completely, but I wanted to make this made for the people who are not in this room.” Related Stories News Selma Blair Now Claims Ignorance Was Cause Of Her Vitriolic Rant Against Islam & “Terrorist Supporting Goons” Agencies Selma Blair Parts Ways With Rep Team Including CAA And Narrative PR Blair continued, “It’s called Hineni . Here I am. The thing I couldn’t say two years ago, I’m now saying with a camera crew behind me. It goes to Israel, so people can see why that land is not an abstraction to us. And it talks to people who disagree with me, on camera, and keeps the disagreement in the cut, because you don’t change a mind by only talking to people who already agree with you.” Watch on Deadline Acknowledging the “ ignorance and rage ” of her words at the time, in the wake of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, Blair come under fire in February 2024 for writing in a comment regarding Rep. Cori Bush (D-MO) and Rep. Rashida Talib (D-MI), “Thank you so much. Deport all these terrorist supporting goons. Islam has destroyed Muslim countries and then they come here and destroyed minds. They know they are liars. Twisted justifications. May they meet their fate.” During Thursday’s reception, Blair reflected on the moment. “It offended people, and I did apologize right away. No conditions, no fine print. I meant it then and I mean it now, and I’m leaving the comment there, because the comment was not the story,” she said. “Here’s what happened next. I’ll try to tell it fast, because it happened fast,” added Blair. “The brands I worked with were gone within a day. A few partnerships I’d spent years building were shelved. My agency was gone. My lawyer was gone. My publicist was gone. My book agent was gone. My book publicist was gone. My social media manager was gone. My son’s godmother was gone – my best friend. While some friends in the business quietly stood by me, most of them were gone. And of course, my manager, my supposed friend of thirty years, and a Jew, was gone too. I still don’t know what any of them were thinking. No one returned my calls. I know the phone stopped. Not rang less. Just stopped.” Following Blair’s 2024 comments, her representatives at CAA and Narrative PR parted ways with the actress known for roles in Cruel Intentions , Legally Blonde , The Sweetest Thing and more. Blair was previously the subject of the Discovery+ documentary Introducing, Selma Blair , which explored her multiple sclerosis diagnosis and how she adapted to living with the neurological disorder. title: Ouster Rumors and a Tense Phone Call: Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy’s Final Weeks at Warners
full_text: × Skip to main content By Borys Kit , Mia Galuppo , Aaron Couch October 2, 2026 3:40pm Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy at the premiere of 'Weapons' Gilbert Flores/Variety/Getty Images Mike De Luca began hearing the rumor over a month ago: He and his Warner Bros. film co-head Pam Abdy were on the chopping block. The source of the rumor was not David Ellison, whom the duo had met months earlier and seemed to indicate they would stay on in a post-merger world. No, De Luca was hearing that this was coming from Josh Greenstein, co-chair of Paramount Pictures. Greenstein, according to sources familiar with the meeting, told other executives in a cross-town engagement that he wanted to get rid of Abdy and De Luca. Other sources, also with direct knowledge of the conversation, countered the remark was directed toward the general stability of Warner Bros., and was made in the context of Greenstein vying for a project and peacocking Paramount’s own superior stability and executives. Regardless, De Luca, never one to sit on his hands, decided to go head on and called Greenstein. “Are you seriously saying this?” He demanded to know, according to sources familiar with the conversation. Greenstein denied the accusations and blamed it on a bad game of telephone. Because the deal was still in limbo given the antitrust suit, he was not legally allowed to make personnel decisions. But on Friday, that conversation feels prescient in hindsight as Abdy and De Luca are exiting the studio they have run since 2022. They learned that Greenstein and his co-chief Dana Goldberg would be taking control of both film divisions — and that they were out of a job – just before a Puck report broke the news late Thursday night. It was the end of four years of highs and lows, during which the duo has been the subject of the Hollywood rumor mill, with constant questions about potential ousters and contract renewals, in almost equal measure. They have faced accusations of overspending on movies with limited commercial prospects, like this weekend’s Tom Cruise bomb Digger , and have been hailed as cinema heroes thanks to major box office wins like Sinners and Weapons, and for bringing home best picture for One Battle After Another . For months leading up to the merger, De Luca and Abdy believed they were safe after a meeting with Ellison, in which he suggested they would stay, according to a high-level Warners source. They told people they believed there could be a friendly rivalry between themselves and Greenstein and Goldberg, given that they all had their own relationships with talent and filmmakers. Maybe the competition could even inspire each other to be better. “Clearly a lot has changed since then,” says the Warners source. Now, De Luca and Abdy are left to plot their next moves. A year ago, they signed a five-year contract renewal through 2030, which they will be paid for. They have told associates they could go to Netflix, and De Luca is said to have grown close with Netflix mogul Ted Sarandos during a series of conversations they had when the streaming giant was tipped to buy Warner Bros. late last year. Could they help Netflix move more into the theatrical space? Could they bring their auteur-driven philosophy to the streamer, which counts middle of the road movies like Carry-On and Red Notice as among its most viewed movies ever? “All of their relationships are theatrical relationships. You aren’t going to convince those filmmakers to go make their big streaming movie,” cautions one source who has business with both Warners and Netflix. “If I were Ted, I’d say, ‘Come over, I’ll give you a sweetheart deal, and help us think through what theatrical could look like.” Netflix showed a willingness to get into the theatrical business when it was going to acquire Warner Bros., and is giving its longest theatrical window ever for its Cannes acquisition La Bola Negra as it hunts for an elusive best picture Oscar. “Netflix’s audience taste is more down the middle. It would be interesting to have them and their more filmmaker-driven approach at Netflix,” says one observer with business at Warners. “I just don’t know if the Netflix audience wants that. They want Red Notice , not May December or Roma or Lost Daughter .” In the weeks since California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced that a settlement with Paramount Skydance would clear the way for a merger, reps and studio execs across the industry expressed doubt that a single executive team could lead the 30-film slate that was laid out in the settlement. Per the agreement, the combined studios must release 30 films for two years and then 32 for the next three years. There are penalties if this threshold isn’t met. For every movie that Skydance falls short of, the studio must pay $30 million to health and pension funds, split among the guilds. Additionally, a judge can force it to sell or spin out Miramax, which was behind the 2026 Paramount Skydance hit Scary Movie. Of course, Goldberg and Greenstein are not completely alone in the oversight of the combined Paramount and Warners film slate, with studio labels actively run by veteran executives. DC Studios, which is still in the middle of a turnaround and coming off of an unfortunate showing with Supergirl , will continue to be led by James Gunn and Peter Safran, while it is believed that Richard Brener is safe for the time being at New Line, home of lucrative franchises like The Conjuring and The Lord of the Rings. And then there is Warner’s newest studio label, Clockwork, the boutique outfit run by a trio of former Neon executives. Clockwork is readying for its first big theatrical release, a remastering of the 1971 British film The Devils , out Oct. 16, and has proved a player at festival markets, landing upcoming film from Sean Baker and Park Chan-Wook. It’s also looking to get into the low-budget genre game. “At the end of the day, you can’t have four chairmen,” says the Warners insider, assessing the notion of De Luca, Abdy, Greenstein and Goldberg all working together. “You can’t share marketing and distribution. You can’t have people fighting over who gets Memorial Day, who gets the Super Bowl ads, and who gets the big spend.” Greenstein and Goldberg’s mandate at Skydance is meat and potatoes and franchise movies, rather than the swings of De Luca and Abdy, known for offering a studio home and big budgets to filmmakers like Paul Thomas Anderson, Ryan Coogler, Alejandro Iñárritu and Emerald Fennell, to varying degrees of commercial success. In this way, De Luca and Abdy’s Warners filled the void left behind when Megan Ellison’s Annapurna, once the place where filmmakers like Anderson could find patronage and distribution, paused its film operations. (Annapurna began reopening its doors for at least some business earlier this year.) And while Neon and A24 have certainly taken up the auteur mantle in the past half-decade, these studios can offer low-to-mid-level budgets, a far cry from the $100 million-plus that De Luca and Abdy greenlit. It is these big swings from name brand directors that will mark De Luca and Abdy’s time at Warner Bros., for better and for worse. There was Sinners , Coogler’s vampire movie that delivered $370 million in ticket sales and Academy Awards glory. Coogler, who took home the original screenplay Oscar , repeatedly credited De Luca and Abdy’s support during the awards campaign, including in his Oscars speech. On the other end of the spectrum, there were films like Maggie Gyllenhaal’s The Bride! ($23.9 million on a $90 million budget), and Cruise starrer Digger , which is tracking to open this weekend to a dismal $8 million to $15 million on a $125 million-plus budget. The detractors categorized the chiefs as overzealous with budgets to the detriment of the larger studio slate, while champions heralded them as Medici-esque in their commitment to ensuring that some of the best films of the past couple of years made it in front of audiences. Hollywood, a town that has never particularly enjoyed any shade of gray, is likely to continue arguing along this binary. Ultimately, it is these strong filmmaker relationships, as well as those with their powerful reps (they are known to be close to CAA’s Bryan Lourd), that De Luca and Abdy will carry with them into their next act. Alex Weprin contributed to this story. THR

title: John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’
full_text: Oct 2, 2026 3:37pm PT John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’ By Marc Malkin Plus Icon Marc Malkin Senior Editor, Culture and Events marcmalkin Latest John Leguizamo Has a Message for David Ellison: ‘Think of What Americans Need and What the Industry Needs’ 15 hours ago ‘La Bola Negra’ Star Guitarricadelafuente to Receive Discovery Award at SCAD Savannah Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Bradley Whitford on Bringing Back ‘The West Wing’ as a ‘Limited Series’ 3 days ago See All Getty Images John Leguizamo is speaking out about the Paramount and Warner Bros. merger, and he’s imploring David Ellison to consider what the industry needs as he takes over the new Skydance. “Come on, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans need and what the industry needs. Think of others for a change.” John Leguizamo has a message for Skydance chief David Ellison: “C’mon, Dave. Do the right thing. Don’t just think of yourself and your pocket. Think of what Americans and the industry needs. Think of others for a change.” pic.twitter.com/DjEUzXvWja — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026 Although the terms of the merger include Paramount-WBD being prohibited from selling the Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in California for at least five years. Leguizamo said “that’s still not enough.” Related Stories 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation “You got an end date. You got an expiration date. That’s not cool,” he said. “People have to plan for the rest of their lives. They plan for five years, and then what?” Popular on Variety “…The industry belongs in L.A.,” Leguizamo said Friday at the Critics Choice Association’s 6th Annual Celebración of Cinema & Television, where he was honored with the Career Achievement Award. “We need to support it and grow it. Rebuild it and add to it. Not subtract.” John Leguizamo says it’s “despicable” and “heartless” that David Ellison’s Skydance is threatening to move Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery’s film and TV production out of Los Angeles. When Variety’s @marcmalkin brought up the five-year production commitment in Ellison’s… pic.twitter.com/yj2YwtwAcG — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026 In April, Leguizamo was one of more than 4,000 film and TV stars and creatives who signed an open letter opposing Paramount Skydance’s pending acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. “We are deeply concerned by indications of support for this merger that prioritize the interests of a small group of powerful stakeholders over the broader public good,” said the letter, which was published by the New York Times and available on the website BlocktheMerger.com. “The integrity, independence, and diversity of our industry would be grievously compromised. Competition is essential for a healthy economy and a healthy democracy. So is thoughtful regulation and enforcement.” Other signatories included Joaquin Phoenix, Ben Stiller, Kristen Stewart, Robert De Niro, Sofia Coppola, Florence Pugh, Pedro Pascal, Edward Norton, Atsuko Okatsuka, Adam McKay, Alan Cumming, Alyssa Milano, Boots Riley, Bryan Cranston, Cynthia Nixon, Damon Lindelof, David Fincher, Denis Villeneuve, Elliot Page, Glenn Close, Jane Fonda, JJ Abrams, Jason Bateman, John Leguizamo, Lin-Manuel Miranda, Margaret Cho, Mark Ruffalo, Noah Wyle, Patti Lupone, Ramy Youssef, Rosario Dawson, Rosie O’Donnell, Ted Danson, Tiffany Haddish, Tig Notaro, Yorgos Lanthimos and Yvette Nicole Brown. Leguizamo also talked about receiving the Career Achievement Award. “It means they five that to you when you think your career is over,” he cracked, before continuing, “I’ve been in it for four decades, a long time, a lot of sacrifices, a lot of great things, a lot of pain and it feels like, ‘Oh, wow. It was worth for something. People notice and recognize what you’ve done and contributed to cinema.’” John Leguizamo calls “Mission: Impossible — Reckoning” a “bomb so expensive they teach it in business school.” via The Critics Choice Association's 6th Annual Celebración Of Cinema & Television pic.twitter.com/Z7NLXqG8sW — Variety (@Variety) October 2, 2026 He delivered emotional remarks while accepting the award from director Gregory Nava. “I will not be finished until every Latin child in this country can turn on a screen,” he said, tearing up. “When a Latin child in this country can turn on a screen and see their own face, their own name, their grandma’s accent, not getting arrested, not dying in minute nine [of an action movie], just living, just being a whole person, that’s the dream. Keep failing forward and don’t’ let anyone every quiet your voice, including the one inside your head telling you that you’re not good enough. title: Rick Devens on How ‘Survivor’ Prepped Him to Win ‘Big Brother,’ Canceling on James Gunn’s ‘Superman 2’ Cameo and If He’d do ‘Traitors’: “I’m Open”
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All October 2, 2026 3:31pm Rick Devens wins 'Big Brother' season 28. Matthew Taplinger/CBS Logo text On Big Brother , Rick Devens was labeled a reality television icon. After winning season 28 on Thursday night, he definitely has entered “icon” status, becoming the first Survivor player to win Big Brother . His casting was part of a larger twist for season 28 that saw three former reality TV players join a pool of new contestants ; competing alongside Devens was his fellow Survivor 50 opponent and season 45 winner Dee Valladares and Big Brother season 26 alum Angela Murray. Devens himself competed on season 38 and 50 of Survivor . Related Stories Movies James Gunn, Peter Safran to Stay at DC Studios as Brand Takes Key Position at Skydance News Kennedy Center Honors 2026 Sets Date, New Venue The show labeled them icons after they entered the Big Brother house, and the name stuck. So did their strong three-person alliance, which through strategic gameplay and season-long dominance ensured at least one of them would have a real shot at winning the game. Devens ultimately won Big Brother in a vote of six to one from the jury, beating out runner-up Taylor Brown. Plus, the audience also took to Devens, awarding him the title of America’s Favorite Houseguest, which fans vote upon at the end of each season. He’s also the most-winning player from a single season, earning $750,000 from winning the show; the $50,000 prize for America’s Favorite Houseguest; and an extra $10,000 he pocketed during a competition while filming. Below, Devens breaks down why he wasn’t sure if would have won Big Brother if Drew Campbell made it to the final two, his thoughts on season 28 houseguests asserting that the icons had “privileges and advantages” this season, James Gunn revealing he was supposed to make a cameo in Man of Tomorrow , and what competitive reality shows he’d do next ( Survivor part three? Big Brother All-Winners? The Traitors ?). *** After you won the final HOH, you decided to evict Drew. Do you really think that Taylor would have had enough time to flip Lala and tell her, “We’re going to vote for Drew to win”? I really don’t think it would have taken much time. I think if Taylor walked out on stage and said, “Lala, we’re voting for Drew,” Lala would have gone, “Okay. You’ll explain to me later.” I think that’s all it would have taken, because those two were so tight. I was legitimately very concerned about it. Now that the show is over and you potentially had time to talk to everybody, if there was a scenario where Drew was in the final two with you, did the jury tell you they would have voted you to win? No, I didn’t. I haven’t had those conversations. I now know that Drew and Taylor, neither of them were gonna take me to the final two, so that makes me feel better about it. But I haven’t had any conversations about how a Drew, Devens vote would have gone. Wow! So do you really still think that Melody [Morris] and Barrett [Pfeiffer] would have voted for Drew? I think it’s very possible. I think Drew’s and my game was super similar, very intertwined. A lot of the moves we made, we made together. We’d won about the same number of comps. He dragged me to the final three. I would have dragged him to the final two. So I think that they had every right to vote however they wanted. I would be shocked if Melody hadn’t gone for Drew, and then Barrett would have been the deciding vote. And that’s a little closer than a six-one vote. I had to do what I had to do, unfortunately. Rick Devens after winning ‘Big Brother’ season 28. Matthew Taplinger/CBS Let’s go back to when you made it to final three. If there would have been a scenario where it would have been you choosing if Drew or Dee would have moved forward, do you think you would have taken her with you? I don’t. I think I would have cut Dee at final three to not sit next to her, and I think Dee would have cut me at final three to not sit next to me. Two Survivor players: We know each other too well. What elements of gameplay that you learned on Survivor do you think served you best for Big Brother ? On Survivor , everything is so much faster, so you turn a vote at the last second almost out of necessity. Dee and I came on here, and I think a lot of Big Brother is you set your vote, you decide what you’re going to do, and then you just wait ‘til the live show. Whereas her and I would go, “I think we can still flip this. Let’s go work on this.” Even sometimes, to our own detriment, we were just bored and were like, We can flip this. Let’s do it. Why not? Also, I learned on Survivor that there’s no shame in going home early or making a dumb move and getting voted out. Great players do that all the time, so you can’t be afraid of that. On this season of Big Brother , I would make a pitch to someone, and they’d be like, “No.” I think a lot of other houseguests would have gone, Oh, that didn’t go well, not doing that again . Whereas I’m like, I got all week, I’m going to make that same pitch to him tonight, and then I’ll pitch it to him again tomorrow morning . And by the end of the week, so many times they were like, “Okay, I get it, let’s do it.” I think just not being embarrassed and not being scared of going home early is a huge power in games like these. Why do you ultimately think these Big Brother players did not opt to get the icons out at the very beginning of the game? Obviously that was a mistake. Yeah, and then they blame that we had all these privileges and advantages. It’s like, you guys had week two through 11 to come together. There’s 14 of you, there’s three of us. You could have gotten us out at any time, and you didn’t do it. Don’t blame our privilege now. Like, come on. I think some of them made a really good move; the [players] that we were working with, they realized that we were valuable to them, that we were good shields for them, and that’s what we sold them. Others, I think, just didn’t want to make a big splash, didn’t want to put a target on themselves, and that’s obviously something that we weren’t worried about. We made big moves every chance we got, so I don’t know. I’m annoyed that they want to blame us having all this special stuff when they outnumbered us 14 to three, and they had 11 weeks to get us out. I feel like if you wanted us out, you could have gotten us out. Get it together, newbies. What advantage do you think they thought y’all had? Because as somebody who loves reality TV, I would want to get y’all out because you have that knowledge of gameplay, and you have targets on your back coming in. That’s what I feel like. I think they’re like, “You were automatically a three-person alliance,” and it’s like, okay, so all it takes [to vote one of us out] is a four-person alliance. And by the way, if it had been Rachel [Reilly] there instead of Dee, I don’t think we’d be [an] automatic [group of three working together]. I don’t think Angela and Rachel were going to work together. I don’t know if Rachel and I were going to work together. I do think we had an advantage in getting into the BB Time Capsule. [ Writer’s note: Viewers voted which players to send into the BB Time Capsule, where they could earn a punishment or advantage .] But even then, it’s a 50/50 chance of what you’re [going to get]. Actually, a lot of people thought it was random: I’m sure that I saw a pattern in there. I [looked] at the button for five minutes, saw the pattern, and got a power. Three newbies went in there, and two of them came out with punishments. That’s not because we came in with a privilege. I think if anything, we were at a disadvantage. I thought half the house was going to be returning players or players from other shows. Oh, really? Yeah. Why did you think that? Because I thought that would be fair. Give us a chance. You know, half newbies and half returnees. That’s even. Angela Murray, Devens and Dee Valladares at the ‘Big Brother’ season 28 finale. Matthew Taplinger/CBS When did this opportunity or conversation for you to go on Big Brother start? Did it come out of you being on Survivor 50 ? I think it might have, but I don’t know the details, and I don’t think I’m even allowed to talk [about it]. But I think probably if I hadn’t done well or I hadn’t made a splash on 50 , I’d never be here. When you were approached about doing Big Brother , were you game on immediately, or were you like, I don’t know, maybe, maybe not ? I was really hesitant about it. I had always said the one [show] I’m not going to do is Big Brother , because it’s so long. And then it comes up, and I’m like, well, maybe I want to do it, but I was like, I can’t do this to my wife. And I went home to my wife Becca and was like, “Hey, this thing came up. I’m not saying I want to do it,” and she said, “You have to do it. You’re never gonna get this opportunity again.” And I was like, “Wait, what?” So it’s all credit to her that I ended up going into that house and winning the game. You have been away from your phones and the outside world. Something that picked up once you got into the house was James Gunn said that you were supposed to do a cameo for Superman , but you canceled last minute because of Big Brother . Have you spoken with him since you’ve won? I haven’t, not since I won, but I cannot wait. I shouted him out in the house. I was so upset that I couldn’t be there on the set of Superman 2 . My whole family still went, and he apparently treated them amazingly and made it such a special experience for them. He was filming in Macon, [Georgia,] where I’m from. That’s why it was all going to work out. But now, I’m like: James, I will go wherever you are. Let me visit whatever set you’re on. I’m so excited to hopefully meet him and be able to talk some Big Brother and Superman with him. I’m a huge James Gunn fan, even bigger now that he’s shown what a great dude he is. What former Survivor player do you think should go on Big Brother next? I’ve got two. They were both on 50. Rizo [Velovic] and Tiffany [Nicole Ervin] would be absolutely incredible at Big Brother . Both of them would just knock it out of the box. They probably have even bigger targets now because the three Survivor players that have been on have done pretty well. But if anyone could pull it off, it would be those two. Which player from this season of Big Brother should cross over and do Survivor ? It’s got to be Kamu [Kirk]. He’s got the physical to do those rough challenges. He has an amazing social game, and unlike a lot of the houseguests in there, I think he would actually thrive being out in the elements and going through all the suffering. Which show between Survivor and Big Brother would you be more ready to do another season of? Just because of how long it is, it’d be harder to come back to Big Brother until my kids were a little bit older. I don’t want to give up another summer while they’re 12 and nine years old. Whereas Survivor ‘s a little shorter, so I’d probably be more ready to go back to Survivor just because of that. What if the Big Brother team came to you next year and was like, “We’re doing All-Winners.” Would you do that? I’d say, “Can you do it [for] season 33. Can Drew stand in for his dad?” Maybe, yeah. But that would be a tough one to say no to for sure. But the kids made a big sacrifice letting me go, and I made a big sacrifice leaving them behind. So I don’t know that Becca would be as supportive this time. What were those first conversations like with your family when you ran off stage and reunited with them? It was so funny. They were so proud of me, even the kids. It wasn’t like, “Hey, we’re rich. What are we gonna get?” It was like, “You did it! We can’t believe it.” And then they were very emotional, and it turns out the reason they were emotional is because they were upset for Drew. They love Drew, their big brother, and they were not happy with me for cutting Drew. I have a lot to answer for with the Drew thing. They told me some of the funny things that happened with Big Brother while I was gone, that I missed some of their fun social posts, and then immediately it was like we were back in regular life, and they’re just telling me about the latest YouTube video they watched or what video game they’re playing. It’s like Big Brother ‘s a thing of the past already. The cast of ‘Big Brother’ season 28. Matthew Taplinger/CBS If your children came to you one day and said, “I want to play Big Brother or Survivor ,” what would you say? I would say, “Heck yeah! Let me get on the phone with Julie [Chen Moonves]. Let me get on the phone with Jeff [Probst]. We’re gonna try to work this thing out. We have a lot to talk about to prepare you mentally and emotionally before you go in this.” Always need to be prepared that it could not go well, but I think they’d be great. I’d love to see them play. Which one would you suggest or push them to take on first? I’d get them to follow their hearts, but I can tell you this: They both really wanted to play Survivor . And now they’ve watched Big Brother , and they saw all the costumes, they saw that we got fed and that there was a bed, and I think they might both be leaning towards Big Brother now. You have a huge name now in the reality TV space as the first Survivor player to win Big Brother . Would you do any other competitive reality TV shows? One that could definitely be in your future would have to be The Traitors . That’s the next big one, right? I’m open to all invitations. I would love to take Becca on The Amazing Race . I think that we would be maybe not this successful, but very entertaining. I just love playing these games. I feel so much gratitude that I get to play these goofy games that I know people would kill to go and play, and I’ve gotten to do it three times. So if I get to do something else, I’m all ears. *** Season 28 of Big Brother is available to stream on Paramount+. THR

title: Sean “Diddy” Combs Reportedly Ran Fort Dix Prison Cell Like a Luxury Suite With Paid Staff
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kevin Dolak Plus Icon Kevin Dolak View All October 2, 2026 3:22pm Sean "Diddy" Combs Shareif Ziyadat/Getty Images for Sean "Diddy" Combs Sean “Diddy” Combs may not be getting out of prison as soon as expected after a Dateline segment this week detailed the luxe lifestyle the rap mogul has allegedly built behind bars, complete with a team of fellow inmates treated like his personal staff. Since arriving at Fort Dix in October 2025 after more than a year at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, Combs has seen his projected release date bounce around the front half of the 2028 calendar, shifting several times between January and June. It now stands at Jan. 21, 2028. In that time, he has entered a drug rehabilitation program at the New Jersey facility, has been involved in a fight with another inmate, and violated several prison rules while serving a 50-month sentence for Mann Act violations . Related Stories News Tupac Murder Trial Highlights a Persistent Diddy Conspiracy Theory Music Tupac's Murder Case Heads to Trial, 30 Years After Rap Icon's Death A report from NBC News’ Dateline this week indicated that the former near-billionaire Bad Boy founder had extended his luxurious lifestyle to his prison cell, where a crew of incarcerated men has been receiving funds in their commissary accounts in exchange for doing basic chores like making the rapper’s bed, cleaning his toilet and shower, and giving him massages. Some inmates also reportedly cooked him meals outside of the prison’s daily menu. Dateline ‘s reporter said she spoke with several inmate sources inside Fort Dix. One inmate at the federal facility showed NBC News an Instagram account that Combs allegedly had been using to communicate with contacts outside the prison. The profile has no profile picture, but it is followed by Combs’ PR representative. Despite his stint in prison rehab, Combs reportedly has had regular access to alcohol, the antidepressant Remeron, a cell phone, and a tablet, none of which inmates are permitted to have without authorization. The Bureau of Prisons has a policy of not commenting on current inmates. After an eight-week trial over the summer of 2025, Combs was convicted of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution and acquitted of the more serious racketeering conspiracy and sex trafficking charges. After a sentencing hearing in a New York federal courtroom in which his life was laid bare, he was handed 50 months. He and his attorneys are awaiting a decision on their appeal of the sentence. But their client hasn’t been making a case for himself from the inside. TMZ reported on July 24 that Combs was allegedly involved in a fight with another inmate over an insult and was then placed in solitary confinement. The skirmish reportedly pushed his release date back about a month, to Feb. 20, 2028. Combs’ rep did not respond to a request from The Hollywood Reporter on Friday for comment on the Dateline story. Asked about the solitary confinement reports, the rep said he is unable to confirm Combs’ movement out of the general population at Fort Dix and into “the hole,” telling THR , “I can’t know where he is. BOP doesn’t keep us apprised.” THR

title: Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’
full_text: Oct 2, 2026 3:17pm PT Skydance Shuffle: David Ellison Addresses Troops About New Name, Says Adieu to Mike and Pam and Sets Table for ‘Barbie 2’ By Angelique Jackson Plus Icon Angelique Jackson angelique814 Latest Sony in Talks to Land ‘Battlefield’ Video Game Movie From Christopher McQuarrie and Michael B. Jordan 18 hours ago Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy to Depart at Warner Bros. Following Paramount Close 1 day ago Chase Infiniti to Star in Dylan Clark’s ‘Portrait of God’ at Lionsgate With Sam Raimi and Jordan Peele Producing 2 days ago See All Getty Images It’s 102 degrees in Los Angeles, but it’s certainly not a summer Friday on the Paramount lot. The studio is swarming with activity, subplots and preparations for the closing of Skydance ‘s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery next week. The industry is obsessively speculating on who survives the merger to be named to David Ellison ‘s executive leadership team come Monday. But first thing’s first — Ellison addressed his troops on the combined company’s new name. It’s Skydance, same as the company Ellison founded 20 years ago, and will be the parent to existing brands like Warner Bros., Paramount and HBO. “As we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations,” Ellison wrote to staff in a memo obtained by Variety . “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.” Remain they will, though under various layers of oversight. Paramount Pictures leaders Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein will be elevated to an expansive creative post, multiple sources tell Variety , overseeing heads of individual film labels across both companies (like New Line stalwart Richard Brener). With this week’s exit of Paramount+ streaming head Cindy Holland, Casey Bloys is the presumptive ruler of all streaming at Skydance. The company has yet to make anything official. Variety confirmed late Thursday night that Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group heads Pamela Abdy and Michael De Luca are out. The decision shocked them, insiders said, though another power player with knowledge of the duo remarked that if they were surprised, “they’re the only ones.” Their fate has been one of the biggest question marks looming over the entire deal. Timing wasn’t on their side, as the motion picture group stacked dizzying losses for WBD this year (despite a banner 2025). Another source added that Ellison personally spoke to the pair on Friday. Today is thought to be their last day on the Warner Bros. lot in Burbank. While Ellison won’t get the keys to WBD until next week’s formal close, dealmaking activity is surging. Goldberg and Greenstein have been reaching out to key talent at Warner Bros. (like Margot Robbie and her LuckyChap partners) to establish continuity. Another knowledgeable source said that wheels are already turning to lock in a sequel to Greta Gerwig‘s “Barbie,” which we previously reported had flatlined over costs. Keep in mind, Ellison just tapped former Mattel CEO Ynon Kriez to be the co-CEO at the new combined company. Related Stories Cynthia Erivo’s Riveting ‘Prima Facie’ Performance Earns TIFF Standing Ovation 'SNL U.K.' Sets Cynthia Erivo, Danny Dyer and James Norton as Next Hosts “There’s no way ‘Barbie 2’ doesn’t happen,” said the source. Popular on Variety Read Ellison’s full Skydance memo below: Team, I am excited to share the new name of our combined company, Skydance. We chose this name for a few important reasons. First and foremost, as we bring Paramount and Warner Bros. together, we wanted to preserve what has made each of these studios iconic. Both have distinct identities, extraordinary legacies and brands that have resonated with audiences for generations. We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight. Of course, Skydance also carries deep meaning for me. I chose the name for my own studio 20 years ago because I wanted something truly personal that also represented limitless possibility. The personal part came from my love of flight: skydancing is another name for aerobatic flying. The possibility came from the cosmos, which to me represents boundless potential and the large-canvas storytelling of cinema. Even our original logo reflected that idea, with each letter of Skydance representing a planet revolving around the sun. From the beginning, the name was meant to capture what great storytelling can do: transport people to places they might never otherwise go and take us beyond the limits of the world we know — and even our own imaginations. That sense of scale, discovery and ambition feels especially fitting for what we are building today. We have big goals for Skydance, and we intend to pursue them with passion, imagination and a willingness to take smart risks. At the same time, we will honor what makes Paramount and Warner Bros. special — giving both studios the opportunity to grow, tell more great stories and bring those stories to even broader audiences around the world, powered by the scale and capabilities of Skydance. Welcome to Skydance. I couldn’t be more excited about what we’re going to build together.
