title: Tinashe Wants to Challenge the Pop Star Label
full_text: × Skip to main content Tinashe. Paris Helena “The Popstar universe has been building in my mind for a while now,” Tinashe says. The 33-year-old, one of pop’s most forward-thinking acts, is speaking about her latest album, Popstar , which dropped on Sept. 25 and features sixteen tracks. It’s the type of album that Tinashe, who’s been working in the entertainment industry since she was a child, could only make now. “I’ve just reached a place in my life, personally and professionally, where I feel very self-assured and confident in my position,” she tells The Hollywood Reporter on a Zoom, pacing around what appears to be an outdoor patio as she excitedly talks about this next chapter. “Both in the industry and just I guess as an individual.” Related Stories News Wynonna Judd Says Rosie O'Donnell's Claims That She's a Trump Supporter Are a "Complete Assumption" Music Jesse Jo Stark and Deadly Doll Sign With BMG Tinashe wanted Popstar to feel “real and raw and empowered.” The singer left the major label system in 2019, finding success in pursuing the music and creative she wants. It’s been a journey of growth and learning, she admits, but it’s been seven years, so growth is to be expected. Realizing she was able to do this on her own restored the confidence in creativity that she felt she had been losing. Despite the album’s name, she wasn’t trying to box herself into a genre. She’s never wanted to limit herself to one of anything, and she feels her music has always been reflective of that. “The categorization was definitely probably the biggest hindrance to how I think I was perceived to the public and the world,” Tinashe says. Letting go of genre might sound confusing when the album’s named Popstar , but to Tinashe, a pop star is so much more than a genre label. “It’s an energy, it’s an embodiment, it’s an ownership of a space that I want to take up in the world,” she says. Tinashe wants to expand what people think of what it really means to be a pop star. From a technical genre perspective, she’s hoping that pop can continue to feel more expansive. “People, when they think of the genre of pop, they have a very watered down and narrow-minded point of view of what that sounds like and looks like,” she says. “I hope to challenge that.” *** How does DJing fit into the equation for you? There’s a couple ways that I feel like I’ve really connected with DJing. One is just dance music, dance culture, dancing. I really enjoy that. It’s really important, maybe now more than ever, for us to have community. To have connection and these points of connection — whether it be live shows, live spaces or places where people can listen to music together, I think is really important. I really want to continue to bring that energy to as many people as possible, whether it be from my live shows or smaller venues or after parties. It’s just fun. The other element is just the exploration of the genre. I’ve dabbled and explored that genre a lot over the years and that led me to more collaborations in the space and working in the space. That just opens your mind to — again, in the spirit of blending these worlds and blending these genres — I feel like we need more women in this space. We need more Black women in the space. We need more conversation. We need to bring all of these different things that are inspiring to me together and not have them be so in their own lane. To that point, do you see yourself as a DJ separate to how you see yourself as a pop star? Yes, I do. In the same way, but different. When I think of myself as a pop star, it’s an additional skill, an additional tool to my tool belt, versus an entirely separate thing. But that’s what a pop star is to me. You can dance, you sing, you can DJ, you can create music, you can write music, you’re the muse. That’s what it’s all about. Do you find it frustrating ever, for pop music in particular, there’s this idea that it’s something made in a factory and it’s just given to artists? In reality, all of the women like yourself that are in this space are actively involved in creating the music . One hundred percent. That’s one of the things that I’m exploring visually in concept with this album, poking fun at the machine of it all or the perfection. We obviously know the cliches that are involved with being a pop star and being a part of that machine. But I also think people can see behind the curtain now a bit more, and that’s another layer to me of what this album means. By embodying what a pop star is, I can both lean into the spectacle and the show of it all, and I can also reject it and be like, “Fuck you, I am who I am. I might not fit this mold or expectation, but this is still what a pop star is because I said so.” Does it feel nice to be able to take that back into your own hands to decide? A million percent. That was really important for me, just where I am in my life, because when I wanted to write this new project, I really wanted to embody that energy. That was the North star of how the creative came together in my mind. How do you feel about social media these days? It’s played an interesting role in your career. I have a good relationship with social media right now. Sometimes that hasn’t always been the case over the years, but I think now I see it in the same way as this whole album concept. There’s an element of performance that is, I guess, a through line. It’s both known and used as a tool. I think about social media as the performance and about how I’m able to tell the story of this album through the performance of it via social media. That’s how I’ve changed my perspective on it. I find that I have a lot more fun doing that. Whereas, I felt [at times] in the past, there was just way more pressure to, who knows, post more or do whatever. Would you call yourself online or more offline? I’m definitely online. So you’re seeing things? Yeah, I’m online a lot. I think, in terms of my own self-perception of the internet or my place on the internet, I more so enjoy now being a part of conversation for the sake of conversation. And being a part of discourse for the sake of discourse. I think that’s important, whereas, obviously, it’s never fun to be the subject of negative discourse, but I think being a part of conversations is fun. It’s fine, it’s good. How do you feel about the industry now versus when you were first getting started? It’s changed a lot. I think, to be fair, I’m very optimistic about it at this point because I’ve seen how many iterations there are of it. And that leads me to believe that whatever’s happening now will not remain the same. That’s exciting in a way. Where music is going, and how people are going to continue to experiment and try new things, I think that’s really fun. I can’t predict it, and being part of that conversation is fun. Obviously, there’s bad things about it all, but there’s always bad things about it. It’s like, it’s the music industry, man. It’s the wild, wild west. THR

title: Montana Locals Protest Daily Wire’s Pro-ICE Production As Filming Disrupts Businesses With Apparent Dramatization Of Renée Good Shooting
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Zach Bryan Dons “Free Palestine” Shirt For Concert At Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium Pedro Pascal Was Surprised Tony Gilroy Made ‘Behemoth!’ “So Intimate And Healing”: “I Thought You Were Gonna Be Mean” ‘Real Time’: Bill Maher Tells New Skydance Bosses “Don’t Believe What Trump Is Tweeting About Me” View All October 2, 2026 3:12pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Daily Wire's 'Pawn Shop' production in Livingston, Montana sparks protests from locals. Rich Polk/Getty Images for Politicon/Courtesy Keegan Nashan Daily Wire ‘s new pro- ICE movie production has attracted local protesters in Livingston, Montana. Filming under the working title Pawn Shop , the latest project from Ben Shapiro’s Daily Wire and Dallas Sonnier’s Bonfire Legend has upset locals — not just because of its alleged use of blank gunshots, pyrotechnics and a staged car wreck without properly notifying residents and businesses, but because its opening scene appears to dramatize ICE’s fatal shooting of Renée Good in Minnesota back in January. Related Stories News ‘Run Hide Fight: Infidels’: Full Trailer For Jonathan Majors’ Controversial Comeback Movie, Daily Wire Release Date Revealed News Trump Celebrity Supporters: Famous Folks In Favor Of The 47th President Livingston local Brooklyn Wilde, who also works in the film industry as a producer and director, tells Deadline that given how much of a “tight knit small town” Livingston is, “This production crew could have done a lot better with notifying everyone.” Watch on Deadline Deadline has reached out to Daily Wire and Bonfire Legend for comment. Daily Wire's new pro-ICE movie production has attracted local protesters in Livingston, Montana. Filming under the working title 'Pawn Shop', the latest project from Ben Shapiro's Daily Wire and Dallas Sonnier's Bonfire Legend has upset locals — not just because of its alleged… pic.twitter.com/LBCQh4rEkh — Deadline (@DEADLINE) October 2, 2026 Meanwhile, the Livingston Food Resource Center (LFRC) released a statement explaining how the production has impacted its clients, who “already face numerous obstacles to meeting their most basic needs.” The group notes that it is the only resource of its kind in the area, serving one in eight Park County residents, and the production has resulted in an “unacceptable” eight-week low in their attendance. “Since filming began across the street from our building, road closures and armed security guards have increased the barriers to accessing food,” they said. “Our clients deserve to feel unequivocally safe accessing this essential resource.” The LFRC claimed they “were not notified of the plans to film” Pawn Shop in front of their pantry and were only informed about the production when calling the city to inquire. “There was no part of the permit process that allowed us to object or advocate for our clients, as the permit had already been issued and filming was due to start that week,” they added. In response, Wilde has joined fellow concerned locals in protesting the production, chanting “Ben Shapiro is a cuck” and shouting details of Good’s fatal shooting at the hands of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross. “It’s just been people who want to get up and say something,” said Wilde. “And we have a legal right to protest on the street as long as we keep it under 65 decibels, and the cops have been called on us about a dozen times. One of our sweetest protesters was ticketed.” With Rust producer Carter Boehm serving on the production team, the latest collaboration between Bonfire Legend’s Sonnier and Daily Wire comes after their last film, Run Hide Fight: Infidels , was picketed by IATSE. Several crew members walked off over labor issues in South Carolina, shortly before Jonathan Majors was involved in an on-set accident that resulted in his co-star JC Kilcoyne needing stitches “all over his hands” after falling through a window. Deadline has confirmed that the Pawn Shop production is not under an IATSE contract either, while it is under a “conditional start” with SAG-AFTRA. Filming takes place on the set of Daily Wire’s ‘Pawn Shop’ in Livingston, Montana. Courtesy of Keegan Nashan A call sheet seen by Deadline lists Danny Trejo, Harvey Keitel and Henry Thomas among the cast. The synopsis for Pawn Shop reads: “When chaos hits the streets of Minneapolis, a young federal agent is left alone after his partner is seriously hurt and must find a way to survive an increasingly dangerous situation. Seeking shelter inside a neighborhood pawn shop, he becomes trapped with a traditional Hispanic father and his progressive college-age son, forcing three very different men to confront fear, conflicting beliefs and a crisis that tests their courage and humanity.” Having recently filmed in the streets of Livingston, the opening scene appears to recreate Good’s fatal shooting through a sensationalized MAGA perspective, in which writer Jake Harlen describes the character Melanie as “a fat blue-hair.” “The first shot takes Melanie in the neck, below her covid mask. The second in the head, above her covid mask,” the script reads. “Blood SPLATTERS on her PASSENGER’s (40s, female, overweight) forehead and matching covid mask.” In a video of the sequence being filmed, protesters can be heard chanting through a megaphone, “Ben Shapiro is a cuck!” With dangerous stunts involving pyrotechnics, Livingston Fire Department confirmed they were on call, but some locals say they were not properly notified of the sequence taking place in their front yards. Deadline has reached out to the Montana Film Office. Livingston Police Chief Wayne Hard says the department has been contacted with complaints “on a daily basis” since production began. Renée Good “To my knowledge, they have the proper permits,” said Hard. “I don’t know whether or not there was an effort made by the film crew to notify neighboring residents and businesses.” With production scheduled in downtown Livingston through Oct. 10, the Livingston City Commission is holding a special meeting on Saturday at 9am to discuss the handling of the production. Directed by Michael Polish, the latest Daily Wire movie comes after Majors’ protested production, Run Hide Fight: Infidels , a sequel to the company’s 2021 feature debut. Meanwhile, Wilde and fellow protesters have discussed “a counter piece that could distract” from the movie, potentially making a documentary “not only about what they’re doing here, but also potentially tying it back into the tragedy that actually happened.” The filming of Pawn Shop comes as Good’s family filed two federal lawsuits on Thursday against the U.S. government, including a wrongful death claim and a complaint against Stephen Miller, Kristi Noem, Tom Homan and Jonathan Ross, as well as other federal agents. Ross shot Good dead on Jan. 7, 2026, as she attempted to drive away from an ICE operation in Minneapolis, amid the Trump administration’s militarization of major U.S. cities. title: Skydance Putting All 3 TV Studios Under George Cheeks: Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios, PTVS – The Dish
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie Post-Merger Skydance Keeping Both HBO Max & Paramount+ Streaming Brands Skydance Putting All 3 TV Studios Under George Cheeks: Warner Bros. TV, CBS Studios, PTVS – The Dish Shane Paul McGhie & Dasan Frazier To Headline Issa Rae’s Male Friendship Comedy Pilot At HBO View All October 2, 2026 3:05pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc George Cheeks, Channing Dungey, David Stapf, and Matt Thunell Sundance/Courtesy More elements of the proposed post-WBD merger Skydance ‘s executive structure are coming into focus ahead of the Paramount-Warner Bros Discovery transaction closing on Tuesday. As Josh Greenstein and Dana Goldberg are poised to oversee Skydance’s movie studios , Warner Bros and Paramount, another senior executive on Paramount CEO David Ellison’s team, Chair of TV Media George Cheeks , would be doing the same with the combined company’s three TV studios, sources said. (This is being done in streaming too, with HBO’s Casey Bloys in line to run the combo of HBO Max and Paramount+.) Related Stories Executives Josh Greenstein & Dana Goldberg Poised To Run Combined Paramount Warner Bros Film Unit, Setting Up Likely Michael De Luca & Pamela Abdy Exit News Paramount-WBD Will Now Be Called Skydance, David Ellison Reveals As part of his current portfolio, Cheeks oversees CBS Studios , something he has done since joining then-ViacomCBS in 2020, with CBS Studios President David Stapf reporting to him. I hear he will now add oversight of Warner Bros Television and Paramount Television Studios, with Channing Dungey, currently Chairman and CEO, Warner Bros Television Group and US Networks, and PTVS President Matt Thunell both staying on and reporting to him. Watch on Deadline It is part of a role expansion for Cheeks post-merger, which is said to also include some sort of oversight of cable brands on the WBD side. (According to the settlement with the 12 state attorneys general, “Paramount and Warner Brothers are required to continue negotiating their cable packages separately.”) In his current post, Cheeks oversees all linear Paramount networks, including CBS (entertainment, sports and news), MTV, Comedy Central, Nickelodeon and BET. The consolidation makes sense. For instance, Thunell, well-liked by Ellison from their tenure together at Skydance, currently reports to Goldberg who, alongside Greenstein, will have their hands full running both movie studios. There had been some speculation that Dungey, given the size and output of Warner Bros TV and her stature as a top TV executive with clout and connections in the industry, may report directly to the CEOs of the combined company as she does now at WBD. Noah Wyle in HBO Max’s ‘The Pitt’ HBOMAX The move would keep the number of direct reports to Ellison (and now co-CEO Ynon Kreiz) across film, TV and streaming on par with what they were at Paramount Skydance, with Bloys (replacing Cindy Holland, who just stepped down ), Goldberg & Greenstein and Cheeks. The combination also would position the three TV studios for future consolidation. It took Disney six years after the acquisition of Fox assets to fully merge the company’s three TV studios — 20th Television, ABC Signature and Touchstone Television — which was done in two stages. CBS Studios has the most clearly defined lane of the three studios as the primary supplier to CBS (as well as home of Star Trek and an opportunistic third-party seller). As things currently sit, there is some overlap between Warner Bros Television and PTVS. They each have been tasked with mining the IP of their sister film studios (which explained Goldberg’s oversight of PTVS) and have been main suppliers to their sibling streamers HBO Max and Paramount+, respectively. Their common playing area is the open streaming market, as both are actively selling outside and have hits on multiple platforms. ‘Abbott Elementary’ Disney / Sami Drasin Over the past couple of years, Warner Bros Television, historically the largest independent TV studio that produced Friends, ER and The Big Bang Theory , has pulled away from developing for broadcast where it still has hit shows in ABC’s Abbott Elementary and CBS’ Big Bang spinoff Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage and Fox’s sophomore drama Memory of a Killer. That is because networks increasingly stay in-house, which helps makes the economics of broadcast work but essentially shuts out third-party suppliers. It is unclear whether that would change now that WBTV would be vertically integrated with a broadcast network, CBS, for the first time, but CBS Studios is pretty dialed in on the CBS brand and its needs, producing the NCIS and Fire Country franchises, Matlock and Ghosts for the network, as well as Little House On the Prairie for Netflix. Recent WBTV highlights include the continuous success of The Pitt , which just repeated as the winner of the Outstanding Drama Series Emmy , the return of Ted Lasso, and the breakout debuts of Rooster and Big Bang spinoff Stuart Fails to Save the Universe , which have been renewed for Season 2. The studio has coming up the buzzy Harry Potter series. Thunell Frankenstein-ed PTVS last fall when he was tasked with integrating together Skydance Television and all cable production units of Paramount, including Showtime/MTV Entertainment Studios, Nickelodeon live-action and Awesomeness, into the new studio. The company, which produces the entire Taylor Sheridan slate for Paramount+, just scored renewals for both its flagship drama Reacher and its spinoff Negaley . Alan Ritchson as Jack Reacher Jasper Savage/Prime Video While he comes from a legal/business background, Cheeks is known for his creative involvement in the brands he oversees. (He is credited with identifying the franchise potential of CBS’ Fire Country , for example.) In addition to being in charge of CBS Studios for the past six years, Cheeks’ TV studio experience includes a stint as Vice Chairman, NBCUniversal Content Studios. title: 17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More
full_text: Oct 2, 2026 2:26pm PT 17 Best New Movies Streaming in October: ’The Invite,’ ‘Disclosure Day,’ ‘Evil Dead Burn’ and More By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest Ed Sheeran Told U2 He Didn’t Want to ‘Get Into Politics’ on Song About Ukraine’s War With Russia, Says Bono 2 days ago Nicolas Cage Says the Marvel Cinematic Universe ‘Is Becoming a Well-Funded and Glorified WWE’ With 50-Plus Year Olds in ‘Ridiculous Outfits’ 3 days ago Florence Pugh Says ‘Instagram Censored Me’ Over Cornell 7 Posts Addressing Sexual Assault Case: ‘Another Shock That Women Are Censored’ 3 days ago See All Courtesy Everett Collection / ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection / Â©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection October is Halloween movie season, so it’s the perfect time for two of the year’s high-profile horror releases to debut on streaming platforms. “Evil Dead Burn,” the extremely grotesque ninth installment in the long-running franchise, premieres on HBO Max this month and should prove to be a big home viewing hit. For the indie horror lovers, Jane Schoenbrun’s instant cult classic “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” arrives to on Mubi to stream after a buzzy summer run that kicked off at the Cannes Film Festival in May. For non horror lovers, summer movie season tentpoles “Disclosure Day” and “Minions and Monsters” are both arriving on Peacock this October. Neither movie set the box office on fire, but streaming should prove a popular destination to watch the latest Steven Spielberg alien blockbuster and the latest entry in the uber-popular “Despicable Me” franchise. A24’s “The Invite” was a huge success in theaters, meanwhile, and should keep the Oscar buzz when it debuts on HBO Max this month. Check out a full rundown below of the biggest movies hitting streaming this month. The Invite (Oct. 23 on HBO Max) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Olivia Wilde’s acclaimed comedy “The Invite” arrives on HBO Max after earning a sturdy $58 million worldwide at the summer box office. Wilde stars opposite Seth Rogen, Penelope Cruz and Edward Norton in this story of two couples whose uproarious dinner party exposes the cracks in their relationships. Variety named “The Invite” one of the best movies of 2026 so far, calling it a “bravura dinner-party dramedy that’s like ‘Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?’ remade by the Woody Allen of ‘Husbands and Wives.’” Disclosure Day (Oct. 9 on Peacock) Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day” arrives on Peacock after a $241 million run in theaters worldwide over the summer. Heavily touted as the Oscar-winning legend’s return to alien-centric science fiction (he is the master who gave us “E.T.” and “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” after all), the chase thriller casts Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt as a cybersecurity analyst and meteorologist who set out on a mission to disclose the existence of alien life to the world. Colin Firth, Eve Hewson and Colman Domingo co-star. The Death of Robin Hood (Oct. 16 on HBO Max) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection “The Death of Robin Hood,” from “Pig” and “A Quiet Place: Day One” director Michael Sarnoski, casts Hugh Jackman as an aged and battle-weary version of the title character, who now lives in self-imposed exile and is tormented by his past. Robin Hood gets a shot at redemption after befriending an orphaned girl. Jodie Comer, Bill Skarsgård, Murray Bartlett and Noah Jupe also star in the A24 release. Evil Dead Burn (Oct. 2 on HBO Max) Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection “Evil Dead Burn” arrives on HBO Max just in time for Halloween movie season. The third movie since the “Evil Dead” series reboot in 2013 (and sixth film in the franchise overall) is directed by Sébastien Vaniček and stars Souheila Yacoub (“Dune: Part Two”) as a woman looking for comfort from her in-laws after her husband’s death. Their gathering at a secluded house quickly turns into a hellish reunion as the family members turn into Deadites. Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma (Oct. 2 on Mubi) Image Credit: ©Mubi/Courtesy Everett Collection “We’re All Going to the World’s Fair” and “I Saw the TV Glow” director Jane Schoenbrun returned bigger and better than ever this year with the Mubi-backed meta slasher dark comedy “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma.” Hannah Einbinder plays a filmmaker tasked with rebooting a horror movie franchise who gets in over her head when she seeks out the franchise’s original star, played with seductive wit by Gillian Anderson. The movie rocked Cannes in May before earning $8 million worldwide over the summer, making it Schoenbrun’s highest-grossing movie yet. Minions & Monsters (Oct. 28 on Peacock) Image Credit: ©Universal/Courtesy Everett Collection “Minions & Monsters” is coming to Peacock after an underwhelming summer box office run with $523 million, putting it on the lower end of movies set in the “Despicable Me” franchise. However, family audiences are sure to turn out in force for the movie’s streaming debut. Pierre Coffin, the series co-creator and voice of the Minions, and Patrick Delage directed the film, which is set in 1920s Hollywood and follows the Minions as silent movie stars who struggle to adapt to talking pictures. Naturally, chaos ensues when the yellow creatures accidentally release monsters out into Los Angeles. Animals (Oct. 9 on Netflix) Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Ben Affleck directs, co-writes and stars in “Animals,” a Netflix original crime thriller that could continue the Oscar winner’s streaming luck after “The Rip” became one of Netflix’s biggest movies of the year. The synopsis reads: “When their son is kidnapped, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate and his wife find themselves drawn into a web of deception. As they scramble to raise the ransom payment, they’re forced to make choices – and reveal secrets – that could tear their world apart.” The cast also includes Kerry Washington, Gillian Anderson, Adriana Paz, Ray Fisher and Steven Yeun. Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger (Oct. 9 on Disney+ and Hulu) Noel and Liam Gallagher get reflective, philosophical and foul-mouthed in “Don’t Look Back in Anger,” the acclaimed documentary that chronicles the brothers’ highly-publicized reunion and comeback tour in 2025. Cameras were given access to rehearsals, backstage and onstage, while the documentary also includes the first joint interview with the brothers in over 25 years. Sacrifice (Oct. 16 on Netflix) Image Credit: ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection Netflix’s “Sacrifice,” starring the high-profile pairing of Chris Evans and Anya Taylor-Joy, marks the English-language debut of “Athena” director Romain Gavras. Evans plays a movie star trying to launch a Hollywood comeback after a viral meltdown. Taylor-Joy stars as the leader of a group of environmentalist radicals, who crash a black tie gala attended by Evans’ actor. This hostage situation quickly goes haywire. Vincent Cassel and Salma Hayek Pinault also star. Love of Your Life (Oct. 14 on Prime Video) Image Credit: ©MGM/Courtesy Everett Collection Rachel Morrison’s romantic drama “Love of Your Life” earned strong reviews after its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival last month. Margaret Qualley stars as Maya, whose chance encounter with Charlie (Gabriel Basso) “sets in motion a sweeping romance and a future beyond anything she had imagined. When that future is suddenly upended, Maya is sent hurtling toward an unexpected new life — one that will force her to reckon with who she is, what she wants, and how to love again,” reads the synopsis from Amazon MGM. Masterplan (Oct. 16 on Prime Video) Stanley Tucci gets a star vehicle in Prime Video’s original heist movie “Masterplan.” The actor plays “a legendary thief who sets his sights on the Mona Lisa, recruiting two young strangers to help him — Chiara, a sharp Italian cybercrime expert, and Jay, a swaggering French explosives specialist — before revealing they are long-lost siblings… and oh yes, by the way, he is their father,” the synopsis reads from Amazon MGM. The supporting cast includes “The White Lotus” Season 2 favorite Simona Tabasco and Victor Belmondo. V/H/S Mixtape (Oct. 9 on Shudder) “V/H/S Mixtape” is the ninth installment in the long-running horror anthology series and features segments from Ernest Dickerson (“Tales From the Crypt: Demon Knight”), RZA (“The Man With the Iron Fists”), David Moreau (“Mads”) and Renee Zhan (“O Black Hole!”). Musician and director Flying Lotus (“Ash”) contributes music video interludes to the film, and debut filmmaker Tobias Forge contributes a music video. Heavy metal icons GWAR also make a featured appearance. The Housemaid (Oct. 9 on HBO Max) Image Credit: ©Lions Gate/Courtesy Everett Collection Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfried powered “The Housemaid” to a hugely impressive $400 million at the worldwide box office this past winter. title: record 25-minute s…
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow , Zac Ntim September 10, 2026 10:16am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jonathan Glazer, Rachel Szor, Yuval Abraham, James Wilson, Paul Lewis, Ekaterina Ochagavia and Harriet Gugenheim attend the NAZA premiere at Venice Film Festival Carlo Paloni/Getty Images Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s NAZA has landed a sensational 25-minute ovation following its world premiere in competition this evening at the Venice Film Festival. The Israeli directors looked solemn as applause erupted for their documentary exposing the calculated targeting of civilians in Gaza in missile strikes by Israeli military through the testimony of intelligence personnel and soldiers involved in the killing. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor look drawn and solemn amid strong applause for Golden Lion Contender ‘NAZA’ exposing Israeli targeting of civilians in Gaza #VeniceFilmFestival pic.twitter.com/hqyzoZhwHM — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 10, 2026 The 25-minute ovation sets a new record for any movie at a major festival, surpassing the near 24 minutes scored by The Voice Of Hind Rajab at last year’s Venice festival and the 22 minutes scored by Guillermo Del Toro’s Pan’s Labyrinth . It’s comfortably the longest ovation at this year’s Venice. Related Stories News Venice Prize-Winner 'NAZA' Brings Explosive Gaza Exposé to U.S. Theaters - Specialty Preview News International Documentary Association Calls On Israeli Government To Halt "Campaign Of Threats" Against 'NAZA' Directors Fittingly, The Voice of Hind Rajab director Kaouther Ben Hania, who is on the jury this year, and its producer Nadim Cheikhrouha were both in the room. Watch on Deadline The directors were joined b y NAZA producer James Wilson (JW Films), who also took credits on The Voice of Hind Rajab , and executive producer Jonathan Glazer. Wilson and Glazer are also the Oscar-winning team behind The Zone of Interest . Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor receiving rousing response at world premiere for Golden Lion contender with producers James Wilson and executive producer Jonathan Glazer joining applause #VeniceFilmFestival pic.twitter.com/XhxFr6G6Gp — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 10, 2026 As the lights went up members of the audience started unfurling Palestinian flags as well as one or two Lebanese flags. It seemed at one point that security guards were going to force the flag-holders to put them away but appeared to think better of it. Audience members at world premiere at the Venice Film Festival of ‘NAZA’ documenting Israeli military targeting of civilians in Gaza display Palestinian flags and banners in support of Palestine #VeniceFilmFestival pic.twitter.com/FzPuMJgLvy — Deadline (@DEADLINE) September 10, 2026 The Palestinian flag has been a flashpoint at the festival this year amid calls for it to be included in flags flying from the Palazzo del Cinema in recognition of Palestinian directors in the selection. Festival director Alberto Barbera has said parent body the Venice Biennale is prevented from flying the flag because Palestine is not officially recognized as a state by Italy. Barbera was present at Thursday night’s premiere and joined in the ovation as well as warmly embracing both directors. The record applause comes after the film received very strong early notices from critics. You can read them here . Based on interviews with 24 Israeli intelligence officers and soldiers, the documentary exposes the AI, phone surveillance and crude points-based systems deployed by the Israeli military in Gaza to decide targets, Hamas-related or otherwise, and then take them out in their homes regardless of whether children and other family members are likely to be killed in the strike as well. It follows and builds on Abraham and Szor’s No Other Land , winner of the Best Documentary Academy Award in 2025, co-directed with Palestinian filmmakers Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal, documenting Israeli army-backed efforts to erase the West Bank Palestinian villages of Masafer Yatta, while painting a wider picture of Israeli occupation. The title NAZA is taken from the Israeli military’s Hebrew acronym to describe the number of civilians that could die when tallying up an estimated death-toll ahead of a strike. “Our film is showing that the basic targeting unit of the Israeli targeting systems is a family home in Gaza,” Abraham told Deadline ahead of the world premiere. “That’s how it operates. Every building in Gaza, every home in Gaza has a number. The system is designed to locate targets. When they are in civilian spaces, when they go back home, that is one of, for me, one of the most striking revelations of the film. A revelation, of course, that I think should have been known to people by the fact that they should have listened to Palestinians in Gaza who are saying it. But to hear it from the inside for me was quite striking.” NAZA is produced by Guardian Documentaries with JW Films in association with Placeholder Films and Unseen Hand. Mk2 is handling sales on the title. Andreas Wiseman contributed to this report . title: a New York Film Festival screening
full_text: Skip to main content By Jill Goldsmith Jill Goldsmith Co-Business Editor More Stories By Jill Venice Prize-Winner ‘NAZA’ Brings Explosive Gaza Exposé to U.S. Theaters – Specialty Preview NBCU’s Donna Langley On Industry Mergers, Taylor Sheridan, And The Road to 2027 Anonymous Content, Higher Ground Set Feature Adaptation Of James Baldwin Biography View All September 25, 2026 2:57pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clockwise from top left: 'Artificial,' 'You Can See Everything,' 'Godzilla Minus One' and 'A Statement' Neon/A24/Toho International/Sony The New York Film Festival opens Friday night with a lineup featuring great films of 2026 along with heavy-hitting world premieres. Artistic director Dennis Lim insists the global bows are not “the be all, end all,” but if they come he credits the vibrant Big Apple audience. “The New York audience engages with a film in a way that is meaningful to filmmakers and that creates a memorable launch for a film, so I would credit our audience for that,” Lim tells Deadline of this year’s slate, which includes Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc You Can See Everything , NAZA by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and world premieres from Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic Artificial to Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth !, Tom McCarthy’s The Statement and the sequel Godzilla Minus Zero by Takashi Yamazaki. Related Stories Festivals James Gray On Opening The New York Film Festival With ‘Paper Tiger’, Surviving The “Cannes Bubble”, Oscar-Season Hopes And Which Filmmakers Inspire Him – The Deadline Interview Festivals Tom McCarthy’s ‘A Statement’, Jonathan Glazer Documentary ‘Joy Of Joys’ To World Premiere At New York Film Festival Jonathan Glazer , Paul Thomas Anderson and Ava DuVernay will also world premiere new documentaries at this year’s NYFF , which runs through October 12. Watch on Deadline “These films came to us and decided to premiere with us with for different reasons. It just so happens we have a certain number of them this year, which shows that we have proven in the last few years that we can be a pretty good place to launch a film,” Lim says. NYFF’s 64 th edition opens tonight at Lincoln Center’s Alice Tully Hall with James Gray’s Paper Tiger . DuVernay’s 14th , a direct follow-up to her acclaimed 2016 documentary 13th (which opened NYFF that year), is the closing-night selection. Asked to tick down the lineup, Lim says Artificial “was in flux for a while with the change in ownership. When the film was at Amazon we did have conversations about it. It was not going to be a 2026 film. That changed when it landed at Neon” to join the indie distributor’s awards slate. Amazon dropped the nearly finished $50 million film after making a massive investment in Altman’s OpenAI, noting the project would be better served elsewhere. Neon acquired global rights in June. Godzilla , conversely, “came pretty early, long before it was finished. There’s a tremendous amount of intricate effects work on the film. We started the conversation early in the spring. They did not do festivals with the previous film, which was a huge success for Gkids and Toho, and they were interested in doing something different with this one. We saw an unfinished version in the summer and though it would be really fun,” Lim tells Deadline. “The Elizabeth Holmes documentary, obviously, had been in the works for a while. I knew of the existence of the film but was sworn to secrecy when they wanted to have maximum impact in Telluride . It was always understood that it would be a surprise there, and we would announce thereafter.” You Can See Everything from A24 world premiered as a secret screening at Telluride, gobsmacking the audience. The Theranos founder allowed the filmmakers into her San Diego home with unfettered access in 2023 during the days before she reported to prison after being found guilty of defrauding investors. Wrote Deadline’s Pete Hammond in his review : “Nothing seems to be off limits as they agree to be miced-up for at least 12 hours a day, wide-angle cameras in place to get all movements, with other cameras getting closeups. Fielder immerses himself in this weird world as someone she comes to trust, much to his astonishment, becoming so close she asks him along on that last drive to prison.” The doc is Fielder’s feature film directorial debut. His 2023 Showtime comedy The Curse was the first and one of the few television series to world premiere in the NYFF’s main lineup, Lim recalls. NAZA , which world premiered in Venice , was a late addition. The investigation into Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza was shot at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv where the filmmakers interviewed Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers about destruction and loss of life. “Films are not made in vacuum, they are made by people. There has not been another year where I felt the films to be so directly in conversation with the real world, really are tackling contemporary reality head on,” Lim says. “I think whether they are documentaries or fiction, all films emerge from this world that we all live in together, the reality that we share, and they will engage with real world institutions.” This year’s festival has set 119 films — 75 features and 44 shorts – across its Main Slate, Spotlight, Currents and Revivals sections along with a series of talks complementing the lineup. title: Skydance
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Paramount-WBD Will Now Be Called Skydance, David Ellison Reveals Paramount-WBD Deal Architect Gerry Cardinale Says Most Of $6B In Expected Cost Savings Will Not Be From Layoffs David Ellison’s “Coziness” With Donald Trump Is “Way Overstated”, Per Paramount Backer Gerry Cardinale View All October 2, 2026 6:27am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc After the expected close of their merger, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will together be known as Skydance . CEO David Ellison revealed the new name Friday in a post on X . The $110 billion merger is projected to be finalized on Tuesday after a year-long pursuit by Ellison and a two-month delay caused by antitrust lawsuits by 12 states and the Writers Guild of America. Related Stories News Paramount-WBD Merger Is A Go As Judge Approves Legal Settlement, Last Hurdle To Close Executives Ynon Kreiz Anointed Co-CEO Of New Paramount-WBD; David Ellison Says Mega-Studio Is “Transformational Moment For Our Industry” “What once was the peak, is now just the beginning,” Ellison wrote. “Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren’t rewriting history – we’re equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling.” The choice of the name, he said, stemmed from several objectives. One is to preserve the history of Paramount and Warner Bros. as individual entities under the Skydance umbrella. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one. Instead, we wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. – and all our extraordinary brands – to remain in the spotlight.” Watch on Deadline When Skydance acquired Paramount in August 2025, the company wanted to take advantage of Paramount’s familiar consumer brand while also emphasizing Skydance as the corporate parent. That meant the official name was “Paramount, a Skydance Corporation,” which was later streamlined to “Paramount Skydance Corporation.” Before the two large media companies combined, the new entity also faced the legal obstacle of an antitrust lawsuit by 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America, which labeled it an illegal monopoly. The settlement of the lawsuits, laid out in a 5-year consent decree, requires separation of the Paramount and WBD operations in several business areas. It also tries to guard against one of the major studios being dissolved, as has been the fear of merger opponents. Those precautions meant that a name appearing to favor one merger partner over the other would also be a potential problem. In the absence of any official guidance on the name, colloquial handles like “WarnaMount” or “ParaBros” became commonplace. One stark reality of the new identity is that Discovery Communications, which went public in 2008, two decades after the Discovery Channel lit up as a cable network, will now no longer have its name in lights. title: James Gunn & Peter Safran To Stay At DC Studios After Paramount-Warner Bros Merger
full_text: Skip to main content By Anthony D'Alessandro Anthony D'Alessandro Editorial Director/Box Office Editor @AwardsTony More Stories By Anthony Michael De Luca & Pamela Abdy: When They Are Leaving Warner Bros & What’s Next For Them New Line Boss Richard Brener Poised To Jump To Merged Paramount-Warner Bros – The Dish James Gunn & Peter Safran To Stay At DC Studios After Paramount-Warner Bros Merger View All October 2, 2026 9:48am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Story Arc L-R: James Gunn and Peter Safran Getty Images James Gunn and Peter Safran , the bosses of Warner Bros-owned label DC Studios , will continue to lead the film, TV and comic book production hub and do what they do best after Paramount closes its acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery. Once upon a time, the Marvel Cinematic Universe was in Paramount’s hands, having a distribution deal with the comic-book label and launching the megaverse with Iron Man, Thor, Captain America and Iron Man 2. Then Marvel took a hike to Disney, which scooped them up for $4 billion in 2009. With DC, Paramount no doubt gains a massive franchise one-up in its library that already includes Star Trek, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and Mission: Impossible. Related Stories Executives Josh Greenstein & Dana Goldberg Poised To Run Combined Paramount Warner Bros Film Unit, Setting Up Likely Michael De Luca & Pamela Abdy Exit News Paramount-WBD Will Now Be Called Skydance, David Ellison Reveals We hear the duo had a recent meeting with new Skydance co-CEO David Ellison about their future and it went well. Per this morning’s news, all film units, Paramount and Warner Bros, are to report into Paramount Pictures co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein . The future of Warner Bros motion picture chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy remains up in the air at the newly relabeled Skydance entertainment conglomerate; that duo is still in need of a chat with Ellison. Watch on Deadline Gunn has been shooting the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow, set for release on July 9, 2027. The label’s Clayface, about the Batman antagonist, is their first lower-budget genre movie, opens October 23. Warner Bros’ second highest-grossing movie last year was Gunn’s Superman with more than $618 million at the global box office. Also in production at DC is Matt Reeves’ sequel The Batman Part II set for February 18, 2028. This past summer’s Supergirl didn’t go so well, with a global gross of $126.4M. Meanwhile, the DC-HBO Max series Lanterns has been a ratings success. Co-created by Tom King, Damon Lindelof and Chris Mundy, it saw its third episode score a massive 10M global viewers in its first three days — 7M from the U.S. Since Lanterns premiered August 16, the pilot has been seen by more than 20 million viewers worldwide and continues to grow, the company said. The series launched as one of HBO Max’s top titles . Safran and Gunn were appointed to lead DC Studios in October 2022 in a new label strategy orchestrated by WBD CEO David Zaslav to mimic Disney’s production label hub structure of Marvel Studios, Lucasfilm, Pixar, etc., with myriad production heads. It was arguably the first time (unless we count Charlie Chaplin) that a filmmaker, Gunn, did double duty as a studio executive. Safran already had a hot streak at Warners/New Line with the multibillion-dollar The Conjuring franchise and also producing DC franchise titles like Shazam and Aquaman . Safran had produced on Gunn’s 2021 The Suicide Squad movie and its HBO Max spinoff series Peacemaker starring John Cena, which has clocked two seasons. This is all according to sources Friday morning. Paramount and DC couldn’t be reached for comment.
